pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -THEK-, and the initial th is voiceless as in 'thin'. Many learners stress the first syllable or say 'kath-EK-tik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term from psychology and psychoanalysis and carries no positive or negative judgment by itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in academic psychology, psychoanalysis, or literary criticism. You will meet it in discussions of Freud, attachment, or how people invest feeling in objects or ideas. In everyday talk, people say 'emotionally invested' or 'attached' instead.

distinctions.note: Cathartic means providing emotional release or purging, while cathectic means concentrating emotional energy on something. The two words are often confused because they look similar.
Affective is a broad term for anything related to feelings or emotion, while cathectic is narrower and refers specifically to the charging of an object or idea with emotional energy.

examples.everyday: My therapist said my cathectic attachment to my old car was really about my dad, which made me laugh.
examples.professional: In our user research report, we noted that participants showed a cathectic attachment to the legacy interface, which slowed adoption of the new design.
examples.analytical: Freud's account of the libido treats the ego's cathectic investments in objects as dynamic, shifting quantities of psychic energy.

nuance.analogy: Like a battery that charges an object with current, a cathectic investment fills a person, place, or idea with emotional energy.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kathexis, meaning holding or possession, via cathexis, the English rendering of Freud's German Besetzung.
common_mistakes: Confusing cathectic with cathartic, which means emotional release.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second, -THEK-.

cathectic.etymology: Borrowing from Ancient Greek *καθεκτικός* (“capable of retaining”)

senses.definition: The quality of being catholic, universal or inclusive.

core.definition: The quality of being universal or all-embracing; in theology, the universality of the Church across place, time, and people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIS, the third syllable. The 'th' is voiceless, and the 't' in the ending is a flap, so it sounds like 'dee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting breadth and universality; used in theology it can also suggest fidelity to the whole Church.
nuance.usage_note: Used in theological and academic writing, and in discussions of ecumenism. In general speech, 'broad-mindedness' or 'universality' is more usual. Do not confuse it with Roman Catholic identity: the term applies to the Church's universality in many traditions.

distinctions.note: Universality is the general word, while catholicity carries the specific theological sense of the Church's wholeness.
Catholicism refers to the Roman Catholic faith and system, while catholicity is a quality that other traditions also claim.
Ecumenism is the movement toward Christian unity, whereas catholicity is a quality of the Church.

examples.everyday: I admire the catholicity of her taste; she'll read anything from poetry to physics.
examples.professional: The seminary prides itself on the catholicity of its faculty, who come from many denominations.
examples.analytical: Cyril of Jerusalem grounds the Church's catholicity in its geographic reach and in its fullness of doctrine.

nuance.analogy: Catholicity is like a wide-open door: everyone, everywhere, in every age may come in.
nuance.etymology: From Greek katholikos, 'universal,' from kath' holou, 'concerning the whole.'
common_mistakes: Treating it as a synonym for Roman Catholicism.
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of LIS.
Pronouncing 'th' as /t/.
nuance.biblical_note: The word itself is not in the RSV. The idea of a universal people appears in Revelation 7:9, a multitude from every nation, and Ephesians 4:4-6, which stresses one body and one faith. In Matthew 28:19, the disciples are sent to all nations.

traditions.view: Catholicity is one of the four marks of the Church, understood as the fullness of faith and means of salvation, found in communion with the pope and bishops.
Catholicity (sobornost in Slavic usage) is the wholeness of the Church, fully present in each local church united in the eucharistic faith with its bishop, and not defined by papal authority.

Most Protestants affirm the Church as catholic in the Creeds, meaning the universal body of all believers in Christ, often described as invisible. Lutherans and Anglicans stress continuity with the historic church, while the Reformed and Baptists emphasize that the true Church is found where the gospel is preached.

senses.definition: A mechanism for allocating resources centrally, as opposed to leaving it up to the free market.

core.definition: An economic system in which a government, rather than free markets, decides what to produce and how resources are allocated.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PLAN in planning, and the ending is a short 'ing' with no hard g. 'Central' has the short e of 'set' and a light second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in economics, but often politically charged in debate, so the phrase can sound critical or sympathetic depending on the speaker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'central planning' in economics classes, news analysis and political debate, often when discussing the Soviet Union, China or government control of industries. In technical talk people may say 'command economy' or 'planned economy' instead. Bringing it up in casual conversation can start a political argument, so choose your tone carefully.

distinctions.note: Command economy is nearly a synonym, but it stresses government directives to firms, while central planning stresses central control of allocation decisions.
Socialism is a broad ideology about ownership, while central planning is one mechanism for running an economy.

examples.everyday: My uncle says central planning never works, but my cousin thinks the government should set prices for everything.
examples.professional: Our budget process is closer to central planning than to decentralized budgeting, which slows every approval.
examples.analytical: Hayek argued that central planning fails because it cannot gather the dispersed knowledge that prices transmit across an economy.

nuance.analogy: Like one orchestra conductor deciding every note for every musician, instead of letting each player respond to the others.
nuance.etymology: Central from Latin centrum 'center'; planning from plan, from French plan, from Latin planus 'flat'.
common_mistakes: Using central planning to mean any government budget; the term refers to comprehensive control of resource allocation.
Putting stress on the first syllable of planning; it is PLAN-ing.

senses.definition: The act of certifying.
senses.example: The certification of the new lab equipment took three weeks of inspections.

senses.definition: The granting of a certificate.
senses.example: Her certification as a nurse practitioner arrived in the mail last Tuesday.

senses.definition: A professional qualification that certifies a person's ability.
senses.example: You do not possess the certifications required for this post.

core.definition: An official document or process confirming that a person, product, or organization meets a required standard or qualification.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on KAY, and the second syllable of the word is very reduced. Americans say the ti as 'tuh' and often drop the second 'i' in fast speech, so it sounds like 'sur-tuh-fih-KAY-shun' with no strong vowel in the middle syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and positive. It signals credibility, competence, and official approval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use certification for professional credentials such as a project management certification or a cloud certification, as well as for products like organic or energy-efficient labels. In casual conversation people more often say 'I got certified' or 'my certificate.' In a job interview, mentioning your certification is normal and expected.

distinctions.note: Certificate is the physical or digital document; certification is the process of earning or granting it, or the qualification itself.
A license gives legal permission to do something, such as drive or practice medicine; a certification shows that you meet a standard, though it may not be legally required.
Accreditation usually applies to institutions or programs, such as a university, while certification usually applies to individuals or products.

examples.everyday: I finally got my food handler certification, so I can work at the coffee shop on weekends.
examples.professional: Our team lead asked everyone to finish their cloud security certification before the audit next quarter.
examples.analytical: The certification of expertise raises a philosophical question about whether a credential truly guarantees the competence it claims to measure.

nuance.analogy: A certification is like a passport stamp: it does not make you a different person, but it officially confirms something about you that others can check.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin certificare, to make certain, from Latin certus, certain, and facere, to make.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I have a certification of nurse' instead of 'I have a nursing certification' or 'I am a certified nurse.'
Confusing the process with the document, so saying 'Please send me the certification' when you mean the certificate.

senses.definition: (archaic) Cerulean; of a deep rich blue color.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: Deep sky-blue; a literary word meaning the same as cerulean.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ROO, the second syllable. The -eous ending is said as 'ee-us', with the vowel sound of 'see' followed by 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to poetic. It sounds elevated and classical, so it is best reserved for writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use ceruleous. In conversation they say sky blue, and in art or design they say cerulean. Using ceruleous in ordinary talk would sound pretentious. You will find it in older poetry or literary descriptions of the sea or sky.

distinctions.note: Cerulean is the common, widely used form in art and design, while ceruleous is an older, literary variant that sounds more poetic.
Azure is a bright, clear blue often used in poetry, while ceruleous emphasizes a deep, rich blue.

examples.everyday: We joked that the paint was too ceruleous for a bathroom, but honestly it looked great.
examples.professional: The brand guide calls the logo cerulean rather than ceruleous, so the palette stays consistent across print and web.
examples.analytical: Older poets sometimes chose ceruleous to lend a sea or sky a classical, elevated tone.

nuance.analogy: Ceruleous is like an old, formal portrait of the sky: the color is the same as cerulean, but the frame is much grander.
nuance.etymology: From Latin caeruleus, dark blue, sky-colored, from caelum (sky).
common_mistakes: Using ceruleous in everyday speech where cerulean or sky blue is expected.
Confusing ceruleous with cerulean as a noun; cerulean is the common form, while ceruleous is only an adjective.

senses.definition: A series of events, each one causing or influencing the next.
A chemical reaction where the products of the reaction influence the reactants of a following reaction, leading to positive feedback.
senses.example: polymerase chain reaction

senses.definition: A nuclear reaction in which particles produced by the fission of one atom trigger fissions of other atoms.
senses.example: The Manhattan Project produced the first recorded controlled chain reaction.

core.definition: A series of events in which each event causes the next one, often spreading quickly and sometimes getting out of control.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the AC syllable of 'reaction', so say 'ree-AK-shun', not 'ree-ak-TEE-on'. The 'ch' in 'chain' is a soft 'ch' sound, and the 'r' in 'reaction' is pronounced as an American 'r' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it often signals a negative outcome such as a crisis or spreading failure. It can also be positive, as when a donation sparks more donations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in news, business, and everyday talk, and in science classes it has specific meanings in chemistry and nuclear physics. People often say 'set off a chain reaction' or 'trigger a chain reaction' when one small event leads to bigger ones. Friends might say 'Oh no, it's a chain reaction' when one problem keeps causing another.

distinctions.note: The domino effect is a predictable sequence in which each event knocks over the next, while a chain reaction can be less orderly and can amplify itself.
A ripple effect is a gradual spreading of consequences outward through a system, whereas a chain reaction is a tighter sequence of triggered events.
A feedback loop is a process where output returns as input, while a chain reaction is a sequence where each event triggers the next.

collocations: a chain reaction in the market

examples.everyday: I forgot my keys, so I was late, then I missed the bus, and the whole morning turned into a chain reaction.
examples.professional: One misconfigured database query set off a chain reaction of failures across three downstream services.
examples.analytical: A single assumption about market liquidity can set off a chain reaction that turns a local default into a systemic crisis.

nuance.analogy: Like a row of dominoes, except that each falling piece can knock over several more at once.
nuance.etymology: Chain from Latin catena 'chain'; reaction from Medieval Latin reactio, from re- 'back' plus actio 'action'.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'chain' and 'reaction' equally, when the second word carries the main stress.
Pronouncing the ending as 'tee-on' instead of 'shun'.
Using 'chain reaction' for a single linked item; it refers to a sequence of events.

senses.definition: In a usual or expected way; in characteristic manner.
senses.example: She characteristically arrived ten minutes early, with coffee for everyone.

core.definition: In a way that is typical of a particular person or thing, as one would expect from their nature.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RIS, the same syllable as in 'characteristic,' and the ending is 'lee,' not 'lih-kal-ee.' Keep the middle syllables weak and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive, often used to note a predictable trait with a hint of humor or approval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use characteristically in writing and in polite speech to say that someone acted in a typical way, as in 'Characteristically, she volunteered first.' It is not dated, but it sounds slightly formal. In casual talk, people more often say 'so typical' or 'classic.'

distinctions.note: Typically describes how often something happens, while characteristically adds that the behavior reveals the person's nature.
Usually refers to habit or frequency, while characteristically suggests a distinctive trait that marks someone's personality.

examples.everyday: Characteristically, Dave showed up twenty minutes early for the barbecue.
examples.professional: Characteristically, the vendor sent the invoice two weeks after the deadline.
examples.analytical: Augustine characteristically treats evil as a privation rather than a substance, and that choice shapes his whole account of the will.

nuance.analogy: Like a signature on a painting: you expect it, and it tells you who made the work.
nuance.etymology: From characteristic plus the adverb suffix -ally.
common_mistakes: Dropping the second 'ch' sound and saying 'kair-ik-ter-ISS-tik-lee' with a clipped ending.
Using characteristically to mean 'typically' in a neutral sense where it sounds odd, such as for facts with no personal trait.

senses.definition: Part of a website or other network where visitors can converse in typed messages.
senses.example: denizens of cyberspace chat rooms

core.definition: An online space on a website or app where people talk in real time by typing messages.

pronunciation.tip: Stress CHAT, the first word of this compound. Pronounce room with an American r and a long oo sound, not like the drink rum.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest casual social talk, or sometimes anonymity and risk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chat room for typed, real-time online conversation, though younger people and tech workers often say Discord server, group chat or Slack channel. In a video meeting, people say in the chat, meaning the typed message panel. The term may sound slightly dated in technical settings, but it is widely understood.

distinctions.note: A forum holds threaded discussions posted over time, while a chat room is real-time conversation.
A group chat is usually among a set of people who know each other, while a chat room is often open to strangers or organized by topic.
A direct message is private and one-to-one, while a chat room has several participants.

examples.everyday: My son spends his evenings in a gaming chat room talking with people across the country.
examples.professional: We moved customer questions out of the public chat room and into our support ticketing system.
examples.analytical: Early chat rooms allowed anonymous talk that made it easy for people to explore identities they would not show in person.

nuance.analogy: A chat room is like a crowded coffee shop with one big whiteboard: everyone can write at once, and the conversation moves fast.
nuance.etymology: From chat (from chatter, informal talk) and room; the online sense developed with early networked systems.
common_mistakes: Saying in the chat room for a video meeting; Americans say in the chat for the typed message panel.
Stressing room too strongly; the main stress falls on chat.

senses.definition: A person who chatters; a chatterbox.
(dated) Any of several passerine birds, mostly from South America; especially the cotingas.
senses.example: In the old natural history book, the chatterer was listed among the colorful birds of Brazil.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A person who talks a lot in a light, idle, or noisy way; a chatterbox.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on CHAT. The middle t is a flap, and the final -er is a reduced, rhotic syllable that sounds like 'er,' not 'air.'

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; it suggests idle, pointless talk rather than warm conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chatterer mostly in writing, especially fiction or older prose, and rarely in speech. In everyday talk most people say chatterbox instead. The word also names a group of South American birds, used mainly in ornithology and bird-watching.

distinctions.note: Chatterbox is informal and playful in tone, while chatterer is more literary and less conversational.
Talker is neutral and can be positive, but chatterer suggests light, unimportant talk.

examples.everyday: Don't sit next to Linda at the reunion; she's a chatterer, and you'll hear about her cruise for an hour.
examples.professional: We need a few careful speakers on the panel, not just chatterers who fill the time with small talk.
examples.analytical: A philosopher might distinguish the chatterer, who fills silence with words, from the thinker, whose words follow from a judgment.

nuance.analogy: A chatterer is like a faucet that keeps running whether or not anyone needs the water.
nuance.etymology: From chatter, which is of imitative origin, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using chatterer in everyday speech, where chatterbox sounds more natural.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'air' instead of a reduced 'er.'

senses.definition: Hot sauce.
senses.example: She drizzled chili sauce over her scrambled eggs, which her father always found too spicy.

core.definition: A thick, sweet and tangy tomato-based condiment with peppers and spices, usually mild rather than hot, used on meat, eggs and fries.

pronunciation.tip: In American speech the main stress falls on CHIL in 'chili,' and 'sauce' gets a lighter secondary stress. The 'ch' sounds like 'chair,' and the second syllable of 'chili' is a short 'ee,' not 'eye.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, everyday food word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American grocery stores and diners, chili sauce means a sweet, mild, tomato-based condiment, similar in texture to ketchup, and it is different from hot sauce like Tabasco or Sriracha. Americans may use it with meatballs, cocktail sauce mixes, or as a dip for eggrolls. If you want something spicy, ask for hot sauce or chili garlic sauce instead.

distinctions.note: Hot sauce is thin and very spicy, while American chili sauce is thick, sweet and mild.
Ketchup is smooth and sweeter, with a looser texture, while chili sauce has chunks of peppers and more spice.
Chili oil is made by infusing oil with dried chilies, so it is oily and often very spicy, unlike the tomato-based chili sauce.

examples.everyday: Can you pass the chili sauce? These fries need a little something.
examples.professional: We need to order twelve cases of chili sauce for the cookout menu next month.
examples.analytical: In American grocery aisles, chili sauce is a sweet, tomato-based condiment, quite unlike the thin, fiery hot sauces of Mexico.

nuance.analogy: Chili sauce is like a friendly cousin of ketchup who has learned a few spices, not a fiery relative of hot sauce.
nuance.etymology: Chili comes from Spanish chile, from the Nahuatl word chīlli.
common_mistakes: Assuming chili sauce is hot and spicy, when in the US it is usually sweet and mild.
Spelling it chilli or chile when Americans write chili, the standard US spelling.

senses.definition: Encoded or encrypted text.
senses.example: All ciphertexts look alike; that's how you know they're in code.

core.definition: Text that has been encrypted, so it cannot be read without the correct key.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SY, and reduce the second syllable to 'fer.' Don't say 'SIP-her-text,' because the 'ci' is pronounced like 'sy' here.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used in computing and security.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ciphertext' in cybersecurity, programming, and cryptography. Ordinary people usually say 'encrypted' or 'scrambled' data. The opposite term is 'plaintext' or 'cleartext,' which means readable text before encryption.

distinctions.note: A cipher is the algorithm or method for encryption, while ciphertext is the output that results from applying it.
A code replaces whole words or phrases with other symbols, while a cipher works on letters, characters, or bits.

examples.everyday: Don't bother trying to read that message, it's just ciphertext without the key.
examples.professional: The logs show the API returns ciphertext, so the client has to decrypt it with the session key.
examples.analytical: A secure cipher should produce ciphertext that reveals no detectable pattern, even when the plaintext is highly structured.

nuance.analogy: Like a locked box: the contents are there, but nobody can read them without the key.
nuance.etymology: From cipher plus text; cipher comes from Medieval Latin cifra, from Arabic sifr, meaning zero.
common_mistakes: Using 'ciphertext' for any random or unreadable code, when it refers only to encrypted plaintext.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'sip' instead of 'sy.'

senses.definition: A term often conflated with begging the question in philosophy.
senses.example: Many people treat circular argument and begging the question as identical, but philosophers distinguish them.

senses.definition: An argument which commits the logical fallacy of assuming what it is attempting to prove.
senses.example: Your claim that the Bible is true because it says so is a circular argument.

core.definition: An argument whose conclusion is assumed in its premises, so it proves nothing. It is a form of begging the question.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AR in argument, while circular keeps a lighter secondary stress on SUR. The -ular ending reduces to 'ler', so avoid full vowels like 'SIR-kyoo-lar'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling an argument circular is a criticism that the reasoning proves nothing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in debates, classrooms, op-eds and online arguments to say that someone's reasoning depends on its own conclusion. In casual speech people often say 'That's circular' or 'That's circular reasoning.' A natural reply is to ask for independent evidence, such as 'What proves that without using the claim itself?'

distinctions.note: In American usage these are nearly synonyms, but begging the question names the fallacy of assuming the conclusion in a premise, while circular argument describes the looping structure of the whole argument.
A tautology is a statement true by its form, like 'a bachelor is unmarried'; a circular argument is a reasoning chain that smuggles its conclusion in, and it can look persuasive.

examples.everyday: He says the movie is great because everyone loves it, and everyone loves it because it's great. That's a circular argument.
examples.professional: Your validation is a circular argument, since we can't call the model accurate because it matches the labels it was trained on.
examples.analytical: Any defense of Scripture's authority that presupposes Scripture's authority to prove it commits a circular argument, leaving the question exactly where it began.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog chasing its own tail: it runs hard and moves a lot, but never gets anywhere.
nuance.etymology: Circular comes from Latin circularis, from circulus 'small circle'; argument comes from Latin argumentum, from arguere 'to make clear, prove'.
common_mistakes: Calling any weak or badly supported argument circular; the term means specifically that the conclusion is assumed in the premises.
Stressing circular fully as 'SIR-kyoo-lar' instead of 'sur-kyuh-ler' with a reduced final syllable.

senses.definition: The property of being clever.
senses.example: Her cleverness with statistics impressed the review board, which hadn't expected such creative modeling.

senses.definition: Something clever, or done cleverly.
senses.example: That trick with the spreadsheet formulas was a cleverness nobody on the team had seen before.

core.definition: The quality of being quick-minded, skillful, or resourceful in thinking or solving problems.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak, r-colored vowel, so say 'KLEV-er-nus' with the er barely heard.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, meaning intelligence and skill. It can turn negative when it suggests cunning, trickery, or showing off.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cleverness to praise a smart idea or solution, as in a clever workaround in a software project. It can also suggest someone is too pleased with their own smartness or is being sneaky. In casual speech, people often say smart or clever instead of using the noun form.

distinctions.note: Intelligence is general mental ability; cleverness is the quick, inventive use of that ability in a specific situation.
Wisdom involves good judgment and moral insight; cleverness can be shrewd without being wise.
Cunning emphasizes deceit or craftiness for personal gain; cleverness can be harmless or admirable.

examples.everyday: I have to admit, the cleverness of that tent design surprised me when I saw how fast it went up.
examples.professional: The cleverness of the caching strategy cut our query time in half without adding new servers.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers distinguish cleverness, the skill of finding means to ends, from wisdom, the judgment about which ends are worth pursuing.

nuance.analogy: Cleverness is like a good shortcut on a hike: it gets you to the top faster, but it is only worth much if you chose the right trail.
nuance.etymology: Clever comes from Middle English, probably from a Scandinavian source, meaning handy or skillful; cleverness is formed from clever with the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using cleverness with a plural or article incorrectly, as in 'a cleverness' when the sense is an abstract quality; say 'a clever idea' instead.
Confusing clever with clear or clean, which share a similar first sound.

senses.definition: Arranged according to close-packing.
senses.example: The spheres in the crystal are close-packed, so the lattice has very little empty space.

core.definition: Arranged so that items sit as tightly together as possible, with little or no empty space between them.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on PACKED, and close is pronounced with an s sound. The -ed ending is a plain t sound after the k, so it's pakt, with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: This term is mainly used in technical fields such as crystallography, materials science and the mathematics of sphere packing, where a close-packed lattice has a specific geometric meaning. In everyday American speech, people say 'tightly packed' or 'crammed' instead. Outside technical writing, it can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Tightly packed is general everyday language, while close-packed has a precise geometric and crystallographic meaning.
Densely packed emphasizes high density or number per unit of space, and can be used in general contexts, while close-packed describes a specific regular arrangement.

examples.everyday: The seats in the old theater were close-packed, so I could barely stretch my legs.
examples.professional: In the materials group, the metal atoms form a close-packed lattice, so the simulation uses a face-centered cubic cell.
examples.analytical: The mathematician argued that the densest arrangement is a close-packed configuration, since any gap lowers the overall density.

nuance.analogy: Like oranges stacked in a grocery store display, each one nestled into the gaps between those below.
nuance.etymology: Close (from Latin clausus, shut) combined with packed, from pack; the compound describes an arrangement with minimal space between items.
common_mistakes: Writing the adjective as 'closepacked' or as two separate words without a hyphen before a noun.
Using close-packed in everyday speech, where 'tightly packed' sounds more natural.
Stressing close as the main syllable, when the stress normally falls on the second element.

senses.definition: Within a shorter distance.
senses.example: Come closer, my dear.

senses.definition: Someone or something that closes.
senses.example: In our organization, the VP of Sales usually acts as the closer.

senses.definition: Someone or something that concludes.
senses.example: The DJ chose a fantastic track as his closer at the end of the night.

senses.definition: Synonym of close (“the point at the end of a sales pitch when the consumer is asked to buy”).
senses.example: The salesman waited for the closer, then asked whether she wanted the premium package.

senses.definition: The last stone in a horizontal course, if smaller than the others; a piece of brick finishing a course.
senses.example: The mason set a closer at the end of the course, cutting the brick to fit the gap.

senses.definition: A horse that performs best toward the end of a race.
senses.example: That horse is a closer, so jockeys hold it back until the final quarter mile.

senses.definition: A relief pitcher who specializes in getting the last three outs of the game.
senses.example: They brought their closer in for the ninth.

core.definition: At a shorter distance; nearer to a person, place or thing, or more emotionally connected to someone.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final -er is an American r-colored vowel, so don't pronounce it as 'closs-ah' or 'closs-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes distance or relationship without any strong emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use closer in everyday requests like 'Come closer' or 'Move a little closer'. In sports, closer is also a noun for a relief pitcher who finishes games in baseball. In sales, a closer is a salesperson who gets the customer to sign.

distinctions.note: Nearer is more formal or literal and is often used for physical distance, while closer is more common in everyday speech and also has emotional senses.
More closely refers to attention or detail, as in 'look more closely', while closer refers to distance or relationship.

examples.everyday: Can you move a little closer? I can't hear you over the music.
examples.professional: Let's take a closer look at the churn numbers before we present them on Friday.
examples.analytical: The passage draws closer to the question of divine presence when it turns from narration to prayer.

nuance.analogy: Like a telescope sliding into focus, bringing a distant object into clear view.
nuance.etymology: Comparative form of close, from Latin clausus meaning shut, with the comparative suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using 'closer to' with 'than' when the comparison is incomplete, as in 'closer than me'.
Confusing the adverb 'closer' with the adjective 'closed' in a sentence about distance.
Saying 'more closer', which is a double comparative and sounds incorrect.

senses.definition: A male hairdresser.
To cut or style hair.
senses.example: She booked an appointment to coiffeur her hair before the wedding.

core.definition: A male hairdresser, especially at an upscale salon; the verb, rarely used, means to cut or style hair.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, FUR, as in French. Americans pronounce the r clearly, so do not reduce the ending to 'oor' or 'yoor'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly pretentious, suggesting a fashionable or upscale salon.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use coiffeur in everyday talk; they say hairdresser, stylist, or barber. The word appears in fashion writing, in French-themed salons, and when someone wants to sound refined. Used casually, it can sound affected, so save it for a formal or witty moment.

distinctions.note: Hairdresser is the ordinary word and works for any gender; coiffeur sounds more French and upscale.
A barber mainly cuts men's hair with clippers or a razor; a coiffeur may cut and style any hair, usually in a fashion salon.

examples.everyday: The wedding planner recommended a coiffeur downtown, and my hair turned out perfect.
examples.professional: We are hiring an independent coiffeur for the photo shoot, so please send her the call sheet.
examples.analytical: The coiffeur's craft, like the tailor's, shapes how a person is seen, so it belongs to the study of appearance and identity.

nuance.analogy: A coiffeur is to hair what a tailor is to clothes: a skilled craftsman who fits the style to the person.
nuance.etymology: From French coiffeur, from coiffer 'to dress the hair', from coiffe 'headdress'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'yoor' or 'oor' instead of 'fur'.
Using coiffeur in casual conversation, where it can sound overly formal or pretentious.

coiffeur.etymology: Borrowed from French *coiffeur*, from *coiffer*, from Old French *coife*, from Late Latin *cofia* (“cap”).

senses.definition: To occupy exactly the same space.
senses.example: The two squares coincide nicely.

senses.definition: To occur at the same time.
senses.example: The conference will coincide with his vacation.

senses.definition: To correspond, concur, or agree.
senses.example: Our ideas coincide, except in certain areas.

core.definition: To happen at the same time, to match exactly in position or pattern, or to agree with something in meaning or result.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the last syllable, 'SIDE,' and keep the 'in' short, like 'in.' Do not make the 'i' in 'co' or 'in' a long sound, and say 'koh' for the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes timing or agreement without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coincide in both everyday and formal speech, especially for timing: 'Our birthdays coincide.' In casual talk, people often say 'happen to line up' or 'fall on the same day.' In writing and meetings, 'coincide with' is common and polished.

distinctions.note: Correspond means to match or agree in meaning, pattern, or relationship, while coincide focuses on exact sameness of time, place, or outcome.
Overlap means partially shared, while coincide suggests that two things line up exactly or nearly so.

examples.everyday: Our flights happen to coincide, so we can share a ride to the airport.
examples.professional: The launch date coincides with the quarterly review, so we should move the demo to next week.
examples.analytical: Her argument coincides with Hume's view that causal inference rests on habit, though she reaches it by a different route.

nuance.analogy: When two things coincide, they are like two transparent sheets laid exactly on top of each other: every line matches.
nuance.etymology: From Latin coincidere, from co- (together) and incidere (to fall upon).
common_mistakes: Using 'coincide' as a noun; the noun is 'coincidence.'
Saying 'coincide to' instead of 'coincide with.'
Confusing 'coincide' with 'coincidence' in speech, where the stress and vowels differ.

coincide.etymology: From French *coïncider*, from Medieval Latin *coincido*, from *con-* + *incido*, from *in-* (“into, to”) + *cado* (“to fall, fall down, drop”).

senses.definition: Simultaneously; at the same time.

core.definition: At the same time as something else; simultaneously. This form is nonstandard; in standard English use simultaneously, at the same time, or concurrently.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, IN. The -ly ending is pronounced lee, with a long e, not lie.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in meaning, but a native reader may see the spelling as an error for coincidentally, which can lower the impression of care in writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always use coincidentally for 'by chance' and say 'at the same time' or 'simultaneously' for timing. Most dictionaries mark coincidently as nonstandard, so avoid it in professional writing. If you need the meaning in a memo, write 'at the same time' or 'simultaneously.'

distinctions.note: Coincidentally, the standard adverb, means by chance; coincidently is the nonstandard form that tries to mean at the same time.
Simultaneously is the standard, precise word for the exact same moment, and is clearer in professional writing.
Concurrently suggests overlapping activities over a period, such as two projects running at once.

examples.everyday: Two buses pulled up to the stop coincidently, so nobody knew which one to take.
examples.professional: The two server migrations were scheduled coincidently, so the on-call team could not cover both at once.
examples.analytical: Because the two reforms were enacted coincidently, historians cannot separate their effects on the economy.

nuance.analogy: Like two runners crossing the finish line in the same instant, with no one ahead.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from coincident and the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using coincidently for coincidentally, the standard form meaning by chance.
Stressing the wrong syllable: koh-IN-suh-dunt-lee, not koh-in-SI-dent-lee.
Choosing coincidently in professional writing where simultaneously or at the same time is clearer.

senses.definition: To develop symptoms or signs of (an illness).
senses.example: With a scratchy throat and a cough, it feels like I'm coming down with a cold.

senses.definition: To lay down (money) in payment; to pay.
senses.example: He came down with five thousand dollars in cash for the used truck.

core.definition: To start getting an illness, such as a cold or the flu, with symptoms appearing gradually.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DOWN, and with is weak, so it sounds like 'wih' or 'wuh' and is nearly unstressed. The th is voiced, so it does not sound like 'wit'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes getting sick.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use come down with in everyday talk to say someone is getting sick: 'I think I'm coming down with something.' It is more casual than get sick and works well when you are not sure what the illness is. It is also common in messages to coworkers, such as 'Sorry, I came down with a cold, so I'll work from home.'

distinctions.note: Catch means to get an illness, often one that others have; come down with is more casual and suggests the sickness is starting to appear.
Get sick is the plainest and most neutral way to say you became ill; come down with suggests a gradual onset.

collocations: come down with a stomach bug

examples.everyday: I think I'm coming down with a cold, so I'm skipping the gym tonight.
examples.professional: Sorry, I came down with a bad stomach bug, so I can't make the 10 a.m. standup.
examples.analytical: Researchers track when participants come down with symptoms to estimate how the virus spreads through households.

nuance.analogy: It's like a storm front arriving: you notice the first signs before the full weather hits.
common_mistakes: Dropping with and saying 'come down the flu'; the phrase needs with.
Saying 'come down a cold' instead of 'come down with a cold'.

conversation.text: I think I'm coming down with a cold.
Half the office came down with the flu last week.
She came down with something on vacation, so she stayed in the hotel.

senses.definition: In a comfortable manner.
senses.example: I snuggled comfortably into the blankets.

senses.definition: Easily; without effort or difficulty.
senses.example: She finished the marathon comfortably ahead of her target time, still smiling at the finish line.

core.definition: In a relaxed, at-ease way, or easily, with enough room or time to spare.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is reduced, and the final 'ly' sounds like 'blee'; do not pronounce the 'p'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests ease, safety, or a clear margin rather than barely making it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'comfortably' in everyday talk about money, time, or sitting. Saying 'We got there comfortably early' means you had extra time to spare. It is also common in sports and business to mean winning or succeeding with a clear margin.

distinctions.note: Easily stresses lack of difficulty, while comfortably stresses having enough room or a safe margin.
Physically refers specifically to the body, while comfortably is broader and can refer to money, time, or sitting.

examples.everyday: We got to the airport comfortably early, so we had time for coffee before the flight.
examples.professional: We are comfortably within budget for the quarter, so we can fund the new hire.
examples.analytical: The model outperforms the baseline comfortably, although the gap narrows on the most difficult subset.

nuance.analogy: Comfortably is like parking your car with a few feet to spare: you do not have to squeeze in.
nuance.etymology: From 'comfortable' with the adverb suffix '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'p' as in 'comp-for-ta-bly'.
Using it to mean 'easily' in situations where no sense of margin or ease is involved.

senses.definition: To exchange substantially; to abate but not abolish completely, a penalty, obligation, or payment in return for a great, single thing or an aggregate; to cash in; to lessen.
senses.example: to commute tithes into rentcharges for a sum

senses.definition: To reduce the sentence previously given for a criminal offense.
senses.example: His prison sentence was commuted to probation.

senses.definition: To pay out the lumpsum present value of an annuity, instead of paying in instalments; to cash in; to encash.
senses.example: The retiree decided to commute her pension annuity into a single lump-sum payment.

senses.definition: Of an operation, to be commutative, i.e. to have the property that changing the order of the operands does not change the result.
senses.example: A pair of matrices share the same set of eigenvectors if and only if they commute.

senses.definition: To regularly travel from one's home to one's workplace or school, or vice versa.
senses.example: I commute from Brooklyn to Manhattan by bicycle.

senses.definition: To journey, to make a journey.
senses.example: Every morning, she commutes across the river to reach the hospital.

senses.definition: To pay, or arrange to pay, in advance, in a lump sum instead of part by part.
senses.example: to commute the daily toll for a year's pass

senses.definition: A regular journey between two places, typically home and work.
senses.example: My daily commute takes almost an hour each way on the freeway.

senses.definition: The route, time or distance of that journey.
senses.example: The commute from our suburb to downtown is about twelve miles.

core.definition: To travel regularly between home and work or school, usually by car, bus, train or bike, on a set schedule.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MYOOT, and the first syllable is a weak schwa. The final t is a clear, crisp t, not a flap, because it is stressed. The noun is COM-mute, so the stress shifts between the verb and noun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound tired or annoyed when people talk about a long commute.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use commute for regular trips to work or school, as in 'I commute forty minutes each way.' It is common in everyday talk, office chat and job listings. Do not use it for a one-time trip; say 'go' or 'drive'. In legal English, 'to commute a sentence' means to reduce it, but that is rare outside courtrooms.

distinctions.note: Travel is general movement from place to place; commute is repeated trips between home and work on a regular schedule.
Drive names the means of travel; 'I commute by bike' is natural, but 'I drive by bike' is not.

examples.everyday: I commute to downtown Denver every day, so I listen to podcasts for about an hour.
examples.professional: Half our team commutes from the suburbs, so we moved the stand-up to 10 a.m.
examples.analytical: The model treats the decision to commute as a trade-off between housing costs and travel time.

nuance.analogy: Like a train running back and forth between two stations on a fixed timetable.
nuance.etymology: From Latin commutare, 'to change altogether,' from com- plus mutare, 'to change'.
common_mistakes: Using it for one-time trips: 'I commuted to the airport yesterday' sounds odd; say 'went'.
Stressing the first syllable as COM-mute, which is the noun pattern.
Confusing it with 'compute' (to calculate), which sounds similar.

conversation.text: My commute is about forty minutes each way.
She commutes into the city by train every day.
Working from home saves me a two-hour commute every day.

senses.definition: Able to be compared (to).
senses.example: An elephant is comparable in size to a double-decker bus.

senses.definition: Similar (to); like.
Constituting a pair in a particular partial order.
senses.example: Six and forty-two are comparable in the divides order, but six and nine are not.

senses.definition: Having comparative and superlative forms.
senses.example: "Big" is a comparable adjective because it can take the forms "bigger" and "biggest"; "unique" and "amazing", in contrast, are not comparable adjectives.

senses.definition: Something suitable for comparison.
senses.example: Find a comparable for the house that sold last month in our neighborhood.

core.definition: Similar enough in size, quality or kind to be compared or treated as roughly equal.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, KAHM-, and the later syllables are weak, sounding like 'ruh-buhl'. Many learners stress the -RAB- instead and say 'com-puh-RAB-ul', which sounds wrong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a fair match and carries no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use comparable constantly, in speech and writing, for prices, salaries, housing and products. The usual phrase is 'comparable to' or 'comparable with', meaning similar in quality or value. In casual talk you might say 'about the same as' or 'similar to', but comparable is also normal in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Similar means alike in some ways; comparable means similar enough in the relevant respects to be compared fairly.
Equal means the same in amount or value; comparable allows real differences as long as the things are roughly the same kind.
Equivalent is stronger and more technical, meaning interchangeable; comparable says they are close enough to weigh against each other.

examples.everyday: The hotel is nice, the rooms are comparable to what we paid last time, and it's cheaper.
examples.professional: Our revised compensation is comparable to market rates for senior engineers in the Bay Area.
examples.analytical: Thucydides presents the Athenian and Spartan decisions as comparable choices, so the reader must weigh the reasons on both sides.

nuance.analogy: Comparable things are like two runners in the same race: different in style, yet fair to rank side by side.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin comparabilis, from Latin comparare 'to compare'.
common_mistakes: Using comparable with from instead of to or with; the usual American forms are comparable to or comparable with.
Stressing the last syllable, saying the word as 'kahm-puh-ruh-BUHL' instead of stressing the first syllable.

comparable.etymology: From Middle English *comparable*, from Middle French *comparable*, from Latin *comparābilis*.

senses.definition: In a compatible manner.

core.definition: In a way that works well together without conflict, especially for devices, software, or ideas that must function as a set.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PAT, and the middle syllables are reduced, so the word ends with a light 'blee' sound. Do not add an extra vowel between the 'b' and 'l' sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes technical or practical fit and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'compatibly' mostly in technical and business writing, such as software documentation or product descriptions. In casual speech people more often say 'work together' or 'work with' instead, since 'compatibly' can sound stiff. It is the adverb of 'compatible', so you can use it after verbs like 'work', 'run', or 'function'.

distinctions.note: Together means working or happening at the same time or place, while compatibly stresses that the things fit well and do not conflict.

examples.everyday: These two apps do not work compatibly on older phones, so check the settings first.
examples.professional: Make sure the new API version runs compatibly with the existing data pipeline before we release it.
examples.analytical: Justice and mercy, in her account, can coexist compatibly within a single moral vision.

nuance.analogy: Working compatibly is like two puzzle pieces that snap together without forcing, with no gap and no overlap.
nuance.etymology: From compatible, from Medieval Latin compatibilis, with the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'compatibly' in casual speech where 'work well together' sounds more natural.
Confusing 'compatibly' with 'comparably', which means 'in a way that can be compared'.

senses.definition: The act of complaining.
senses.example: customer complaints

senses.definition: A grievance, problem, difficulty, or concern.
senses.example: I have no complaints about the quality of his work, but I don't enjoy his company.

senses.definition: In a civil action, the first pleading of the plaintiff setting out the facts on which the claim is based.
senses.example: The plaintiff's complaint alleged that the company breached its contract and caused financial losses.

senses.definition: In criminal law, the preliminary charge or accusation made by one person against another to the appropriate court or officer, usually a magistrate.
senses.example: The officer filed a criminal complaint with the magistrate after the assault.

senses.definition: A bodily disorder or disease; the symptom of such a disorder.
senses.example: Don't come too close; I've got this nasty complaint.

core.definition: A statement that you are unhappy about something, or a formal report of a problem to a company or authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PLAY, and the final -nt is a clean cluster with no extra syllable. Do not add a vowel and say 'kum-PLAY-nit.' The t is often unreleased in relaxed speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it implies that something is wrong. It is neutral in formal settings such as filing a complaint with an agency.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'd like to file a complaint' or 'I have a complaint' in formal settings, and 'make a complaint' is also common. In everyday talk, 'Any complaints?' or 'No complaints' is a casual way to ask whether something is fine. 'No complaints' is positive and means 'I'm happy with it.'

distinctions.note: Grievance is more formal and often refers to a workplace or union issue, while complaint is broader.
Criticism is a reasoned judgment, often professional, while complaint is an expression of dissatisfaction.
Ailment is a health problem, often chronic, while in medicine complaint means a symptom reported by a patient, as in 'chief complaint.'

examples.everyday: Any complaints about the food? Everything's great, thanks.
examples.professional: We received a complaint from a client about the delayed invoice, so I'm escalating it to finance.
examples.analytical: Her central complaint is not that the system is unfair, but that it offers no way to hear her objection.

nuance.analogy: A complaint is like a warning light on a car dashboard: it tells you something needs attention, but not what caused it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French complaint, the noun from complaindre (to lament), from Latin complangere.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make a complain' or 'a complain'; the noun is complaint.
Using complaint as a verb, as in 'I complaint the waiter'; the verb is complain.
Saying 'I have a complaint' with an aggressive tone in a shop; soften it with 'I'm sorry to bother you, but...'

complaint.etymology: From Middle English *compleynte*, from Anglo-Norman *compleint*, from Old French *compleindre*, eventually from Latin *planctus* (whence *plaint*).

senses.definition: To address or greet (someone) formally with expressions of courtesy, respect, etc. to give or pay (someone) a compliment (etymology 1, noun sense 2).
senses.example: The mayor complimented the visiting ambassador with a formal greeting at the airport.

senses.definition: To express a favorable opinion of (someone); to praise.
senses.example: Her manager complimented me on my presentation, saying the data story was clear and persuasive.

senses.definition: To give (someone) a thing (such as a gift, or an academic degree or title) as a sign of courtesy or respect.
senses.example: The university complimented her with an honorary doctorate for decades of work on public health.

senses.definition: To congratulate (someone).
senses.example: My colleagues complimented me on passing the certification exam after months of late-night study.

senses.definition: Followed by away: to surrender (something) while giving or paying compliments.
senses.example: The swindler complimented the old widow away from her life savings with honeyed words and smiles.

senses.definition: Followed by into: to put (someone or something) into a certain situation or state while giving or paying compliments; also, followed by out of: to deprive (someone) of a thing while giving or paying compliments.
senses.example: The salesman complimented the shopper into buying a second jacket she never needed.

senses.definition: To give or pay compliments.
senses.example: She compliments people sincerely, which makes her easy to work with on any team.

senses.definition: To congratulate.
senses.example: Our department chair complimented the team on launching the model ahead of schedule.

senses.definition: An expression of a favorable opinion about someone.
senses.example: to pay someone a compliment

senses.definition: A formal act or expression of congratulation, courtesy, respect, etc. also in the form compliments: formal expression of congratulation, courtesy, respect, etc. complimentary language; flattery, praise.
senses.example: Her kind compliment about my dissertation made the long revision process feel worthwhile.

senses.definition: A thing given as a sign of courtesy or respect; a gift, a present.
senses.example: The conference organizers left a small compliment in each room, a box of local chocolates.

core.definition: A kind remark or expression that praises someone or something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHM, and the middle syllable reduces to 'pluh'. As a verb the final syllable is pronounced -ment with more stress, KAHM-pluh-ment. Don't confuse it with complement, which sounds the same but means something that completes.

nuance.connotation: Positive; a compliment is meant as praise, though sarcasm can change its meaning depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans give compliments all the time in casual conversation, such as 'That's a great jacket!' Common replies are 'Thanks!' or 'Thank you, that's so nice.' Don't deny it or say 'no, it's nothing,' which can sound awkward; accepting warmly is the American norm. Compliments on appearance are fine with friends, but personal comments about someone's body can seem intrusive at work.

distinctions.note: A complement completes or goes well with something; a compliment is praise. The spellings distinguish them.
Praise is broader and can be formal or public; a compliment is usually a short, personal remark.

examples.everyday: Your garden looks amazing this year, I'd love to know your tomato secret.
examples.professional: The client gave the team a real compliment on the dashboard, so let's share it with the group.
examples.analytical: A compliment can express admiration while also quietly setting a standard the speaker expects the listener to meet.

nuance.analogy: Like a small gift of attention: short, often free, and a way of showing you noticed something good.
nuance.etymology: From French compliment, from Italian complimento, a courtesy; its roots go back to Latin complere, to complete.
common_mistakes: Confusing compliment with complement, which sound the same in American English but mean different things.
Using the noun stress on the verb; the verb is pronounced KAHM-pluh-ment.
Replying 'no' or 'it's nothing' to a compliment, which can sound awkward; say 'thank you'.

compliment.etymology: Borrowed from French *compliment* (“expression of respect, compliment”), from Italian *complimento* (“expression of respect, compliment”), from *compimento* (“completion, fulfilment”), from Latin *complēmentum* (“that which completes or fills up,…

conversation.text: Thanks for the compliment. You made my day!
She complimented my shoes on the train this morning.
"You look so young!" "I'll take that as a compliment."

senses.definition: Capable of being composed (as from multiple constituent or component elements).
senses.example: The software team built the app from composable modules that snap together easily.

core.definition: Able to be put together from separate parts or components in many different ways.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, the same syllable as in 'compose.' The final '-able' is reduced to 'uh-bul,' not pronounced as a full 'ay-bul.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies flexibility and good design.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'composable' in software and technology conversations, such as 'composable architecture' or 'composable commerce.' It is also used informally for modular furniture or products that can be arranged in different ways. In everyday talk, 'modular' or 'flexible' is more common.

distinctions.note: Modular means divided into self-contained units. Composable adds the idea that those units can be combined in many different ways.
Compatible means things can work together without conflict. Composable means they are designed to be assembled into new wholes.

examples.everyday: My new sofa is composable, so I can set it up as an L-shape or as one long couch.
examples.professional: Our platform team wants everything built as composable microservices that teams can reuse.
examples.analytical: A composable system is one whose overall behavior can be predicted from the behavior of its parts when they are combined.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of building blocks: each piece is simple, but you can assemble endless structures.
nuance.etymology: From compose, from Latin componere 'to put together,' plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'COM-puh-zuh-bul.'
Confusing it with 'comparable,' which has a different meaning and stress pattern.

senses.definition: Uncontrolled or reactive and irresistible.
senses.example: Jenny is a compulsive liar—don't believe a thing she says.

senses.definition: Having power to compel; exercising or applying compulsion.
senses.example: Critics argued the agency's compulsive powers allowed it to seize documents without any court review.

senses.definition: One who exhibits compulsive behaviors.
senses.example: A compulsive often knows the behavior is harmful, yet feels unable to stop.

core.definition: Done repeatedly and impossible to control, often even when you know it is harmful or unnecessary.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PUL, and the final syllable -sive is a short 'siv', not a long 'seev'. Keep the first vowel as a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes behavior that is unhealthy or out of control, though people use it casually for habits like cleaning or organizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use compulsive in everyday talk to describe habits, such as 'compulsive shopper' or 'compulsive cleaner.' In a medical or psychological setting it has a more precise meaning. Calling someone a compulsive shopper can be teasing among friends but hurtful in serious conversation.

distinctions.note: Obsessive describes thoughts that keep coming back. Compulsive describes actions that someone repeats to relieve the anxiety those thoughts cause.
Habitual means done regularly without much thought and can be harmless. Compulsive implies a loss of control and often harm.

examples.everyday: My brother is a compulsive snacker, so he always keeps a bag of chips in every drawer.
examples.professional: Some developers are compulsive about code reviews, and they end up blocking releases over trivial style issues.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that compulsive behavior is best understood as a failed attempt to restore a sense of control.

nuance.analogy: Compulsive behavior is like a car stuck in a loop on a racetrack: it keeps circling even when the driver wants to stop.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin compulsivus, from compellere, meaning 'to drive together' or 'to force'.
common_mistakes: Using compulsive as a synonym for compulsory, which means required by rules.
Using compulsive for something you simply like a lot in serious settings, which can sound inaccurate or unkind.

compulsive.etymology: Borrowed from French *compulsif*, formed from Latin *compulsus*, past participle of *compellere* (“to compel”), from *com-* (“together”) + *pellere* (“to drive”).

senses.definition: The science and technology of machines that see, concerned with the theory for building artificial systems that obtain information from images, such as a video sequence, views from multiple cameras, or multi-dimensional data from a medical scanner.
senses.example: Computer vision helps the hospital software detect tumors in scans of patients' lungs.

core.definition: The field of AI concerned with enabling computers to interpret and understand images and video, such as recognizing objects or faces.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on PYOO, and vision is pronounced with a zh sound, like 'measure', followed by a reduced 'un'. Do not say it as 'VIZH-shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is a respected research field with many practical applications, so people usually talk about it with interest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term for both the research field and the technology it produces, such as face unlock or quality inspection in factories. In job postings and team talk, people often say 'CV' for computer vision, which can confuse people who read it as curriculum vitae. A natural reply to 'What do you work on?' is 'Mostly computer vision, for medical imaging.'

distinctions.note: Image processing transforms or enhances images, such as sharpening or filtering, while computer vision extracts meaning and understanding from them.
Machine learning is a general set of methods for learning from data, while computer vision is an application area that often uses machine learning on images.

examples.everyday: My phone uses computer vision to recognize faces when I unlock it.
examples.professional: Our computer vision team is training a model to flag defects on the assembly line in real time.
examples.analytical: Computer vision raises philosophical questions about what it means to see, since a machine may classify images without any understanding of them.

nuance.analogy: Computer vision is like teaching a machine to glance at a photo and say what matters in it, the way a radiologist reads a scan.
nuance.etymology: 'Computer' comes from compute; 'vision' comes from Latin visio, from videre, 'to see'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing vision as VIZH-un with the wrong stress, or as VIJ-un.
Using CV without context, since in many American workplaces it can also mean a resume.

conversation.text: Computer vision teaches machines to interpret images and video.
Our computer vision model inspects welds on the production line.
Computer vision is how your phone finds all the photos of your dog.

senses.definition: The process or act of calculation.
The use of a computer or computers.
The study of computers and computer programming.
senses.example: This course will cover several major fields of computing.

core.definition: The use of computers to process information, or the study of how computers work and are programmed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PYOO, and the ending is a short, unstressed 'ing' sound, not 'eeng'. The final ng is one nasal sound; don't add a separate g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. In career and education contexts it sounds professional and positive, as in 'computing skills' or 'computing jobs'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'computing' broadly, as in 'cloud computing', 'personal computing' or 'I studied computing in college'. In everyday talk people usually say 'computers' or 'tech' instead, since 'computing' sounds more formal. In schools, 'computer science' is the standard name for the academic field, and 'computing' is the more general term.

distinctions.note: A computer is the machine itself; computing is the activity or field of using or studying such machines.
Computation is a specific calculation or the process of calculating; computing is broader and covers use, programming and systems.

examples.everyday: My daughter wants to major in computing, so she's taking a coding class this summer.
examples.professional: Our team moved the reporting pipeline to cloud computing, which cut the processing time roughly in half.
examples.analytical: As a discipline, computing asks not only what machines can calculate but what counts as a meaningful procedure at all.

nuance.analogy: Like cooking in relation to a kitchen: it is the activity that the equipment makes possible.
nuance.etymology: From compute, from Latin computare, to reckon together, plus the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a strong 'PYOO-ter' instead of the reduced 'kuhm' at the start.
Using 'computing' to mean the machine; say 'computer' or 'computing device' for the hardware.
Using 'a computing' as a countable noun for a device; the word is normally uncountable.

senses.definition: In an argument or syllogism, the proposition that follows as a necessary consequence of the premises.
senses.example: The conclusion of the syllogism follows necessarily from the two premises we accepted.

senses.definition: The end, finish, close or last part of something.
senses.example: The conclusion of the concert was a stirring rendition of the national anthem.

senses.definition: The outcome or result of a process or act.
senses.example: The conclusion of the year-long study was that the new drug reduced symptoms.

senses.definition: A decision reached after careful thought.
senses.example: The board has come to the conclusion that the proposed takeover would not be in the interest of our shareholders.

senses.definition: Arrangement; settlement.
senses.example: Both sides hoped for a quick conclusion to the lease dispute before winter.

senses.definition: The end or close of a pleading, for example, the formal ending of an indictment, "against the peace", etc.
senses.example: The prosecutor's indictment closed with the conclusion that the defendant acted against the peace.

senses.definition: An estoppel or bar by which a person is held to a particular position.
senses.example: The court ruled that the company's earlier filing created a conclusion barring its later claim.

core.definition: A judgment or decision reached after reasoning, or the final part that ends something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the klu syllable. The -sion ending is pronounced zhun, like the s in vision, not shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound positive when it shows a clear result, but it can sound final or closing in a dispute.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'What's the conclusion?' in both casual and work talk, and the idiom 'jump to conclusions' means judging too quickly. In meetings people often say 'the bottom line' instead, but conclusion is common in reports and presentations. 'In conclusion' opens the last part of a speech or essay, and a natural reply to 'What's your conclusion?' is 'My conclusion is that we should wait.'

distinctions.note: A conclusion is the final claim, while an inference is the process of drawing it, often from indirect evidence.
A result is any outcome, while a conclusion is a judgment about what the outcome means.

examples.everyday: I don't want to jump to conclusions, but he might have missed the train.
examples.professional: Based on the A/B test, we can draw the conclusion that the new checkout page improved conversion.
examples.analytical: The argument's conclusion does not follow from its premises, because the sample was far too small to support a general claim.

nuance.analogy: Like the final number on a calculator after all the steps have been entered.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conclusio, from concludere, meaning to end or close.
common_mistakes: Saying make a conclusion; the usual verbs are draw or reach a conclusion.
Pronouncing -sion as shun; in this word it is zhun.

conclusion.etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French *conclusion*, from Latin *conclūsiō*, from the past participle stem of *conclūdō* (“to conclude”), from *con-* + *claudō*, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **kleh₂w-* (“key, hook, nail”).

senses.definition: In a confused manner.

core.definition: In a bewildered, unsure way, showing that you cannot think clearly or do not understand what is happening.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FYOO, and the first syllable is a weak 'kuhn'. The '-ed' sounds like a short 'id' in this adverb, and the final '-ly' is pronounced 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, because it describes bewilderment or confusion in a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adverb in speech and mostly meet it in fiction or formal writing. In everyday talk, say 'in a confused way' or 'looking confused' instead. A writer might describe someone who 'glanced around confusedly' at a crowded room.

distinctions.note: Confusingly describes what makes something hard to understand, while confusedly describes a person acting bewildered.
Uncertainly stresses doubt about what to do next, while confusedly stresses a muddled and unclear state of mind.

examples.everyday: He blinked at me confusedly when I mentioned the meeting had moved to Tuesday.
examples.professional: When I asked for the revised numbers, the vendor just stared at me confusedly and said he would check.
examples.analytical: Many readers respond confusedly to Hume's claims about causation, because the key terms shift from one page to the next.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio tuned between two stations, the mind responds confusedly, catching pieces of several signals at once.
nuance.etymology: From confused (from Latin confundere, 'to pour together, mix up') plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'confusedly' in casual speech, where 'in a confused way' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'confusingly', which describes what makes something hard to understand.

senses.definition: Having the same or very similar nature, personality, tastes, habits or interests.
senses.example: I found my new data science team congenial, since we shared the same curiosity and work habits.

senses.definition: Friendly or sociable.
senses.example: The congenial bartender makes the Hog’s Head an inviting place to hang out during the weekends.

senses.definition: Suitable to one’s needs.
Agreeable to one's disposition.
senses.example: The quiet cabin proved congenial to my temperament, so I stayed there through the long winter.

core.definition: Pleasant and friendly, with people or things that suit your personality, tastes or needs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, JEE, and pronounce the 'ia' as a quick 'ee-ul' sound with no separate 'ah' vowel. Do not confuse it with 'congenital', which has a different stress and ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a warm, agreeable atmosphere or people who fit well together.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'congenial' in formal or polite contexts, such as 'a congenial group' or 'a congenial workspace'. In casual speech, 'friendly' or 'easygoing' is more common. It is a good word for reviews, introductions and professional writing.

distinctions.note: 'Friendly' describes behavior toward others, while 'congenial' describes a pleasant environment or group that suits your personality and tastes.
'Congenital' means present from birth, so the two words share a root but have completely different meanings.

examples.everyday: We had a really congenial group at dinner, so the whole evening went by fast.
examples.professional: The team is pretty congenial, so the code reviews feel more like conversations than critiques.
examples.analytical: A congenial reading of the text emerges when the interpreter shares enough of the author's assumptions to find the argument coherent.

nuance.analogy: A congenial group is like a well-fitting pair of shoes: they feel comfortable and suit you without effort.
nuance.etymology: From Latin congenialis, 'of the same birth or nature', from con- 'together' and genialis 'of birth, generative'.
common_mistakes: Using 'congenial' to mean 'born with', which is the meaning of 'congenital'.
Pronouncing the 'ia' ending as two full syllables, as in 'JEE-nee-AL'.
Using 'congenial' for a single item when 'pleasant' or 'suitable' might be more natural.

senses.definition: A statement likely to be true based on available evidence, but which has not been formally proven.
senses.example: Her conjecture that the server crashed from memory leaks turned out to be correct.

senses.definition: A statement or an idea which is unproven, but is thought to be true; a guess.
senses.example: I explained it, but it is pure conjecture whether he understood, or not.

senses.definition: A supposition based upon incomplete evidence; a hypothesis.
senses.example: The physicist used his conjecture about subatomic particles to design an experiment.

senses.definition: To guess; to venture an unproven idea.
senses.example: I do not know if it is true; I am simply conjecturing here.

senses.definition: To infer on slight evidence; to guess at.
senses.example: We can only conjecture why the sales numbers dropped so sharply last quarter.

core.definition: A claim believed likely true but not yet proven, or an educated guess drawn from incomplete evidence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'JEK'. Americans say the final '-ture' as a soft 'chur', and the verb is pronounced the same way. Don't stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in mathematics and science. In everyday speech, 'mere conjecture' or 'just conjecture' is dismissive, suggesting the claim has no real support.
nuance.usage_note: In mathematics, 'conjecture' is a precise term for an unproven statement that experts believe is true. In everyday American speech, people more often say 'a guess' or 'speculation', and 'that's just conjecture' can sound like a sharp rebuke. As a verb, 'conjecture that...' is formal; casual speakers say 'guess' or 'speculate'.

distinctions.note: A guess can be random or casual. A conjecture is reasoned from some evidence and usually stated more formally.
A hypothesis is a testable proposal for a study. A conjecture is often a broader claim that may be hard to test, as in math.
A theory is well supported by evidence and tested across many cases. A conjecture is still unproven.

examples.everyday: Nobody knows why the printer broke, so that's just conjecture until the tech takes a look.
examples.professional: I wouldn't present that as a finding; right now it's a conjecture until we run the A/B test.
examples.analytical: Fermat's Last Theorem stood as a conjecture for over three centuries before Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.

nuance.analogy: A conjecture is like a map of unexplored land: it shows where you think the road goes, but you haven't walked it yet.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conjectura, 'inference', from conicere, 'to throw together', from com- and jacere, 'to throw'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KON-jek-chur) instead of the second.
Confusing 'conjecture' with 'conjuncture', which means a combination of circumstances at a particular time.

conjecture.etymology: From Old French, from Latin *coniectūra* (“a guess”), from *coniectus*, perfect passive participle of *cōniciō* (“throw or cast together; guess”), from *con-* (“together”) + *iaciō* (“throw, hurl”); see jet.

senses.definition: (usually with "well-"): Having favorable rapport with a powerful entity.
senses.example: The developer got his zoning permit quickly because he was well connected at city hall.

senses.definition: Having relationships; involved with others.
senses.example: She stayed connected to her college friends through monthly video calls.

senses.definition: Involved with organized crime, specifically someone not (yet) working for a crime organization, but referred to as a "friend" by made guys/wise guys inside the organization.
senses.example: Vinny was never a made man, but he was connected and ran errands for the family.

senses.definition: Intimate; having bonds of affection.
senses.example: After the funeral, the two cousins felt more connected than they had in years.

senses.definition: That cannot be partitioned into two nonempty open sets.
senses.example: A space is connected if it cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open sets.
