nuance.analogy: A logistician is like an air traffic controller for supplies, deciding where each shipment goes so nothing collides or runs late.
nuance.etymology: Formed from logistic plus -ician, on the model of mathematician, so that the word denotes one who practices logistics.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'LOJ-ih-stish-un', instead of the -TISH syllable.
Confusing 'logistician' with 'logistics', which is the field, not the person.

senses.definition: The quality of being lognormal.

core.definition: The property of a variable whose logarithms follow a normal distribution, so the data are skewed but log-transformed values look bell-shaped.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MAL, as in 'normality', with a weaker stress on LOG. The vowel in 'log' is the open 'ah' sound in US English, and the final -ity is a reduced 'uh-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise statistical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lognormality' only in statistics, econometrics, finance and quantitative fields. In conversation you would more often say 'the data are lognormally distributed' or 'the logs are normal'. When discussing a dataset with colleagues, a natural remark is 'Is the lognormality assumption holding up?'

distinctions.note: 'Normality' describes data that are normally distributed themselves, while 'lognormality' describes data whose logarithms are normally distributed.
'Lognormal' is the adjective describing the distribution, while 'lognormality' is the abstract noun for the property.

examples.everyday: My coworker says the income data looks very skewed, so we might need to check for lognormality before we go further.
examples.professional: Before fitting the model, I ran a Shapiro-Wilk test on the log-transformed revenue to check the lognormality assumption.
examples.analytical: Claims of lognormality rest on the logarithms being symmetric, and many heavy-tailed datasets fail that test even when a log transform improves the fit.

nuance.analogy: Lognormality is like a stretched-out rubber band: the raw data look lopsided, but when you take the logarithm, the shape evens back into a bell.
nuance.etymology: From log plus normal plus -ity; normal comes from Latin normalis, made according to a carpenter's square.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'lognormality' with 'normality', which describes a different distribution.
Stressing LOG too strongly, as in 'LAHG-nor-mal-i-tee', instead of the -MAL- syllable.

senses.definition: The process or an instance of logging off.
senses.example: Remember to save your work before you do a logoff from the shared lab computer.

core.definition: The act of ending a computer session by signing out of a user account.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of the noun, LOG-off, but stress 'off' in the verb phrase, as in 'I'll log OFF now.' Keep the vowel in 'log' short and open, like 'dog', not like 'low'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a routine technical action with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people usually say 'log out' or 'sign out'. The noun 'logoff' appears mainly in computing, especially Windows, where 'Log off' is an item in the Start menu. Use 'log off' as the verb in careful writing, and say something like 'Are you logged off?' or 'I'll sign out' in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Both mean ending a session; logoff is more associated with Windows and enterprise systems, while logout is common on websites and apps.
Logging off ends your user session but leaves the computer running, while shutting down powers the whole machine off.

examples.everyday: Don't forget to log off before you leave the library computer.
examples.professional: Our policy requires an automatic logoff after fifteen minutes of inactivity on shared workstations.
examples.analytical: The logoff event marks the point at which an authenticated session ends, which makes it a critical boundary for access control.

nuance.analogy: Like locking the door and taking the key when you leave a shared office.
nuance.etymology: From the phrasal verb 'log off', where 'log' means to record, from the ship's logbook.
common_mistakes: Using 'logoff' as a verb in formal writing; the verb is two words, 'log off'.
Putting the main stress on 'off' in the noun; the noun stresses the first syllable, LOG-off.

senses.definition: The written characters used in the common method of writing; opposed to shorthand, or typing or printing; handwriting.
senses.example: Her grandmother still drafts every thank-you card in longhand before sealing the envelope.

senses.definition: Written by hand in normal characters, as opposed to shorthand.
Written by hand (with pen or pencil), rather than printed out; handwritten.
senses.example: I had to write the essay out twice longhand – they wouldn’t let me print it out. It took forever!

core.definition: Written by hand in ordinary letters, rather than in shorthand or typed or printed on a computer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, LAWNG, and the second syllable is short 'hand'. In many dictionaries the stress is shown on the second word, but in American speech the compound stresses the first part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical, descriptive word, sometimes used with a note of old-fashioned craft.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use longhand when they want to contrast handwriting with typing or shorthand, as in 'I wrote the notes in longhand.' It is common in schools, legal settings, and writing about personal habits. Many Americans now write 'by hand' or 'handwritten' in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Shorthand is a special system of abbreviations for fast note-taking, while longhand is ordinary written letters.
Cursive is a style of joined handwriting, while longhand refers to ordinary writing by hand in contrast to shorthand or typing.

examples.everyday: I can't find my phone, so I'll write the grocery list in longhand on the back of this envelope.
examples.professional: Please send me your meeting notes in longhand, since our typed version was missing the key decisions.
examples.analytical: Scholars who transcribe medieval manuscripts often compare the printed edition with the original longhand to check the spelling.

nuance.analogy: Writing in longhand is like hand-drawing a map: the work takes more time, but the line you make is personal and direct.
nuance.etymology: Compound of long and hand; the name contrasts ordinary writing with shorthand.
common_mistakes: Using 'longhand' as a noun for 'cursive', which is a specific style of handwriting.
Putting the stress on the second word, 'hand', rather than the first.

senses.definition: A person on watch for approaching enemy, police, danger, etc.
senses.example: The raid failed when the lookout noticed the enemy group.

senses.definition: A session of watching for an approaching enemy, police, etc.
senses.example: We kept a lookout all night, but nobody came.

senses.definition: A vantage point with a view of the surrounding area.
senses.example: From the lookout on the ridge, we could see the entire valley and the river below.

senses.definition: A subject for observation; a prospect or view.
senses.example: For young graduates in our town, the job market's lookout remains uncertain and rather bleak.

senses.definition: One's perspective, outlook; hence, one's responsibility. (used with a possessive pronoun or a noun in a possessive form).
senses.example: Every person's interest is his own lookout.

senses.definition: An observation window.
senses.example: A small lookout in the prison door let guards watch the cell without entering.

senses.definition: A joist that extends in cantilever out from the exterior wall (or wall plate) of a building, supporting the roof sheathing and providing a nailing surface for the fascia boards.
senses.example: The carpenter installed a lookout beneath the eaves, extending past the wall to support the roof.

core.definition: A person or place from which someone keeps watch for danger, or the act of watching for danger.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, LOOK, and the second syllable has the 'ow' diphthong in 'out'. Don't stress the second syllable as in the phrasal verb look out.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a role or a place of watchfulness, sometimes with an implication of danger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lookout' as a noun for a guard, a watchtower, or a high spot with a view, such as a 'mountain lookout' on a hiking trail. It is also used for a person who watches for danger in a group. Note that the noun is written as one word, while the verb is two words.

distinctions.note: 'Lookout point' or 'scenic overlook' describes a place to admire a view, while 'lookout' can also mean a guard or watch for danger.
A 'watchtower' is a tall structure built for watching, while a 'lookout' can be any spot, including a natural one.

examples.everyday: We stopped at the scenic lookout on the trail to take some photos of the valley.
examples.professional: The security team posted a lookout at the loading dock while the vendor was on site.
examples.analytical: The prophet is figured as a lookout set on a wall, watching for what God will reveal.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighthouse keeper scanning the horizon, a lookout sees trouble coming before anyone else.
nuance.etymology: From look plus out, used as a noun.
common_mistakes: Writing 'look out' as one word when using the noun, or 'lookout' as two words when using the verb.
Stressing the second syllable as in 'look-OUT'.

conversation.text: We hiked up to the lookout and could see for miles.
There's an old fire lookout at the top of the mountain.
Can you be on the lookout for a parking spot?

senses.definition: Synonym of small change (“coins in the pocket, ready to spend”).
senses.example: I had a bit of cash on me, but no loose change.

senses.definition: Synonym of small change (“insignificant amount of money”).
senses.example: The cost of an opulent wedding is loose change to a millionaire.

core.definition: Coins and small bills carried in a pocket or purse, ready to spend on small purchases or parking meters.

pronunciation.tip: Stress CHANGE, the noun, in American speech. Link the s of loose into the next word smoothly, and pronounce change with a clear j at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is casual and everyday, and it can also mean a trivial amount of money.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use loose change in everyday speech for coins one carries, especially when paying for parking or a vending machine. In a phrase such as 'I have some loose change,' it signals casual money on hand. It can also mean an insignificant amount, as in 'That's just loose change to them,' which is a figurative use.

distinctions.note: Spare change is the phrase used when asking someone for money, while loose change is simply coins one has on hand.

examples.everyday: Can you spare some loose change for the parking meter? I only have a card.
examples.professional: Don't worry about those small adjustments; that's loose change next to our quarterly budget.
examples.analytical: Economists often dismiss such sums as loose change, but in aggregate they shape consumer behavior.

nuance.analogy: Loose change is like the crumbs in a jar of quarters: small, scattered and useful at the right moment.
nuance.etymology: Loose from Old Norse lauss; change from Old French changier.
common_mistakes: Using loose change for a large amount of money in a literal sense; it normally means coins or small sums.
Saying 'small loose change' as if loose already means small; the phrase is just loose change.

senses.definition: One who loots, who steals during a general disturbance such as a riot or natural disaster.
senses.example: After the hurricane, before law was restored, looters stole everything that wasn't nailed down.

core.definition: A person who steals goods during a riot, war, natural disaster, or other chaos when normal order has broken down.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle 't' is a flap, so it sounds like a quick 'd', and the final '-er' is a weak r-colored vowel, not a full 'ur'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a looter implies they are exploiting a crisis to take what is not theirs.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'looter' mainly in news coverage of hurricanes, earthquakes, riots, and protests, and in police reports. It is not usually used for an ordinary shoplifter during normal business hours. Americans would say 'thief' or 'shoplifter' for those cases.

distinctions.note: A thief is anyone who steals, in any setting, while a looter specifically takes goods during chaos or disaster.
A shoplifter takes items from a store, usually secretly and in small amounts, while a looter takes large quantities during disorder.
Pillager is a more historical or literary word for soldiers or raiders who destroy and steal from a region.

examples.everyday: My neighbor said the police were patrolling the streets to keep looters away from the damaged houses.
examples.professional: Our security vendor added patrols after reports of looters near the warehouse during the blackout.
examples.analytical: Scholars distinguish between opportunistic looters and those who steal to survive when public services collapse.

nuance.analogy: A looter is like a crow that swoops in and grabs whatever is left unguarded when the owner has run away.
nuance.etymology: From loot plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using 'looter' for an ordinary shoplifter in calm conditions, which sounds unusual to Americans.
Pronouncing the middle 't' as a hard /t/ instead of a quick flap in American speech.

senses.definition: A man whose chief interest is seducing, usually women.
senses.example: Everyone at the office knew he was a Lothario who never stayed with one woman for long.

core.definition: A man who acts charming mainly to seduce women, often moving from one relationship to the next without commitment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, THAIR. Don't pronounce the th as a t; it is the voiced-or-voiceless th sound of 'think' and 'the' used here as a soft th.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a man who treats romance as a conquest and is not sincere, and it is usually said with disapproval or mild humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing or in a teasing way, not as ordinary conversation. Calling someone a lothario implies he is a smooth talker who cannot be trusted with partners. It can describe a real person or a character in a novel or film.

distinctions.note: A playboy lives a glamorous, pleasure-seeking life, while a lothario is specifically focused on seducing women.
Womanizer is the more common everyday word and is more direct and less literary than lothario.

examples.everyday: My cousin says that guy at the party is a total lothario, so be careful with him.
examples.professional: Our marketing manager jokes that the sales rep is a lothario, but he really just charms clients.
examples.analytical: The novel's protagonist resembles the classic lothario, whose seductions reveal more about his vanity than his desire.

nuance.analogy: A lothario is like a fisherman who sees every person as a catch, casting for conquest rather than for companionship.
nuance.etymology: From Lothario, the seducer in Nicholas Rowe's play The Fair Penitent (1703).
common_mistakes: Using lothario as a general word for any man who is friendly; it specifically implies seduction.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: Luxury.
Luxurious, sophisticated.
senses.example: The hotel's lobby had a sleek, luxe feel with marble floors and velvet chairs.

core.definition: Luxury, especially in fashion, design, or marketing; it is also used as an adjective meaning luxurious, as in a luxe hotel.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable that rhymes with 'looks' and 'books'. The French final -e is silent, so don't add a vowel or say 'loo-ZHAY'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and aspirational, though it can sound trendy or marketing-driven.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use luxe mostly in fashion, interior design, and advertising, often as an adjective, as in 'luxe bathroom' or 'luxe-but-casual'. In everyday speech, 'luxury' or 'fancy' is more usual. Using it as a noun to mean luxury is less common and can sound stylized.

distinctions.note: Luxury is the standard noun; luxe is a shorter, trendier term used mostly in fashion and design writing.
Luxurious is the standard adjective for expensive comfort; luxe is more stylized and often used in marketing.

examples.everyday: Their new place has a luxe bathroom, which is way fancier than ours.
examples.professional: The campaign targets a luxe-but-affordable position for the new line.
examples.analytical: The word luxe signals status in marketing copy, so it promises more than the product's materials may deliver.

nuance.analogy: Like the word premium printed on a plain box: it promises something finer than what is actually inside.
nuance.etymology: From French luxe, from Latin luxus, meaning excess or extravagance.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it LOO-zhay as in French; Americans say 'luks'.
Using luxe as a verb; it is only a noun or an adjective.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to a type of poetry (such as a sonnet or ode) that expresses subjective thoughts and feelings, often in a songlike style.
senses.example: Her lyric poetry explores private grief and joy in short, musical verses.

senses.definition: Of or relating to a writer of such poetry.
senses.example: Emily Dickinson is often considered a lyric poet whose work captures intense personal emotion.

senses.definition: Lyrical.
senses.example: The novelist's lyric prose made even a description of rain sound like music.

senses.definition: Having a light singing voice of modest range.
senses.example: The tenor role calls for a lyric voice rather than the heavier dramatic sound.

senses.definition: Of or relating to musical drama and opera.
senses.example: The company's lyric theater season includes Puccini's La Bohème and Mozart's Don Giovanni.

senses.definition: Melodious.
senses.example: The river's lyric murmur lulled us to sleep as we camped beside it.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the lyre (or sometimes the harp).
senses.example: The ancient Greek lyric instrument was played with a plectrum and strung with seven gut strings.

senses.definition: A lyric poem.
senses.example: Her favorite lyric was a short poem about autumn that she memorized in college.

senses.definition: The words of a song or other vocal music.
senses.example: The lyric in line 3 doesn't rhyme.

core.definition: The words of a song, especially in popular music.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a short, reduced 'ih'. The r is clearly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in popular music contexts it is ordinary, while in literary contexts it can sound elevated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'lyrics' in everyday talk for the words of a song, almost always in the plural. 'Lyric' in the singular, used as a noun, usually refers to a single lyric poem and sounds literary. Fans often discuss lyrics when they talk about a song they love.

distinctions.note: 'Lyric' is singular and can mean one line or one poem; 'lyrics' is plural and means the full set of words of a song.
A lyric is a short poem expressing personal feeling, while 'poem' is the broader category.

examples.everyday: Do you know the lyrics to that old country song? I can never remember the chorus.
examples.professional: The marketing team needs the song lyrics cleared before we can use the track in the campaign.
examples.analytical: The poem is a lyric in the classical sense, because it gives voice to a single speaker's inner feeling.

nuance.analogy: Lyrics are like the printed script of a musical play: the words that the melody carries.
nuance.etymology: From Latin lyricus, from Greek lyrikos, 'for the lyre', from lyra 'lyre'.
common_mistakes: Using 'lyric' in the singular when you mean the full words of a song; say 'lyrics'.
Stressing the second syllable (lih-RIK) instead of the first.
patterns: [usually pl.] the lyrics to/of a song

lyric.etymology: From French *lyrique*, or its source, Latin *lyricus*, from Ancient Greek *λυρικός*, from *λύρα* (“lyre”).

senses.definition: A composer of madrigals.
A singer or interpreter of madrigals.

core.definition: A composer of madrigals, or a singer or performer who specializes in performing madrigals.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllables are weak, so say them as quick uh or ih sounds, and keep the r clear. The ending -ist is short, like 'list', not 'leest'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a descriptive term from music history with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use madrigalist in music history courses, concert programs and early-music circles. It refers to a Renaissance specialist, not to any choir singer. Among non-specialists, the phrase 'madrigal singer' is more common for a performer, while madrigalist more often means a composer.

distinctions.note: Madrigal singer refers only to performers; madrigalist can also mean a composer of madrigals.
Choral singer is a general term; madrigalist implies the specific repertoire of Renaissance secular part songs.

examples.everyday: My cousin joined a group that sings old madrigals, so now she calls herself a madrigalist, which made the whole family laugh.
examples.professional: The early music conference featured two madrigalists who discussed how to perform Gesualdo's chromatic writing in a modern concert hall.
examples.analytical: Thomas Morley, as an English madrigalist, adapted Italian forms to the native language, which shows how a foreign genre could be naturalized.

nuance.analogy: A madrigalist is to a madrigal what a playwright is to a play: the person who makes the piece exist, whether by writing it or performing it.
nuance.etymology: From madrigal plus the suffix -ist, meaning one who makes or practices something.
common_mistakes: Using madrigalist for any choir singer; the word refers specifically to the Renaissance madrigal repertoire.
Pronouncing every syllable fully, as in MAD-ree-gal-ist; the middle vowels should be reduced.

senses.definition: A hierarchically structured secret organization engaged in illegal activities like distribution of narcotics, gambling and extortion.
senses.example: Investigators said the mafia controlled the trucking companies and extorted payments from local shop owners.

senses.definition: A crime syndicate.
senses.example: The mafia family expanded into gambling and loan sharking across three counties during the 1980s.

senses.definition: A trusted group of associates, as of a political leader.
senses.example: Critics said the governor surrounded himself with a mafia of loyal aides who guarded access.

senses.definition: An entity which attempts to control a specified arena by violence or threats.
senses.example: moral mafia

core.definition: A secret criminal organization that uses violence, extortion, gambling and drug trafficking to control illegal businesses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending -ia is two quick syllables, fee-uh, not a long fee-ah. Capitalize Mafia only when referring to a specific organization.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies violence, intimidation and corruption.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mafia in news, movies and casual talk, often generically to mean organized crime. Everyday speakers often say mob for the same idea, which is more informal and common. Calling an office clique or a company's internal network a mafia is a joke about control, and it usually gets a laugh.

distinctions.note: Mob is the common American word for organized crime groups and is more informal; mafia usually refers to a specific network with strict internal codes.
A cartel is a trafficking organization, usually focused on drugs; mafia covers a wider range of crimes, including extortion and gambling.

examples.everyday: Did you see that new mafia show? The boss is terrifying, but the costumes are great.
examples.professional: Our compliance team flagged a vendor whose billing looked like a mafia-style protection scheme, so we paused the contract.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the Sicilian mafia was simply a criminal organization or a parallel system of power that filled the gap left by the state.

nuance.analogy: Like a family business that runs on loyalty and fear rather than on contracts.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; probably from Sicilian dialect, first recorded in the nineteenth century.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing mafia when speaking generically; use a lowercase mafia for the general idea.
Using mafia for any group of friends; the word always implies crime or intimidation.

senses.definition: Main course in a meal.
senses.example: For the potluck, my sister brought the roast chicken as the main dish.

core.definition: The principal food served in a meal, such as the meat, fish, or pasta that the rest of the meal is built around.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DISH, with main carrying lighter secondary stress. In fast speech the n of main can run into the d sound, so say it smoothly as one phrase.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, descriptive term used in cooking, menus, and everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say main dish in recipes, potlucks, and when planning a meal: 'What's the main dish?' For menus, restaurants more often say entree, which in the US means the main course, not the starter as in British usage. Main course is also common and means the same thing.

distinctions.note: Main course and main dish are nearly identical; main course is more common in restaurants and formal menus, while main dish is common in home cooking.
In American English entree means the main course; in British English it often means a starter, so Americans can be confused by the British sense.

collocations: the main dish of the evening

examples.everyday: For dinner I'm making a chicken casserole as the main dish, with a salad on the side.
examples.professional: The caterer confirmed that the vegetarian main dish will be served at the six o'clock reception.
examples.analytical: A menu, like a theological system, has a main dish that organizes everything else, so the sides only make sense in relation to it.

nuance.analogy: The main dish is the anchor of a meal, the way a central idea anchors an essay.
nuance.etymology: Main comes from Old English mægen, strength; dish comes from Old English disc, a flat plate or serving.
common_mistakes: Stressing main as strongly as dish; in this phrase DISH carries the main stress.
Using main dish for an appetizer or dessert, which Americans would call a starter or side.

senses.definition: The tallest mast of a sailing ship that has more than one mast; particularly a full-rigged ship.
The second-foremost mast of a non-sailing ship with more than one mast.

core.definition: The tallest and central mast on a sailing ship that has two or more masts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAYN, with secondary stress on mast. Pronounce the final st cleanly, and keep the vowel in mast short, as in 'mass.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise nautical term with a literary or historical flavor.
nuance.usage_note: Only sailors, maritime historians, and readers of sea stories use mainmast in everyday American English. Most Americans would say the big mast or the main mast in casual talk. Ships with several masts are identified by mast order, such as foremast and mizzenmast.

distinctions.note: The foremast is the forward mast, while the mainmast is the largest, central mast on a ship with more than one mast.
The mizzenmast is the mast behind the mainmast on a three-masted ship.

examples.everyday: We could see the sailboat's mainmast from the pier.
examples.professional: The shipyard inspected the mainmast for stress cracks before the voyage.
examples.analytical: In Moby-Dick, Ahab nails the gold doubloon to the mainmast, making the spar a symbol of his obsession.

nuance.analogy: The mainmast is like the spine of a sailing ship, holding up its most important sails.
nuance.etymology: From main (principal) plus mast (upright spar), from Old English mæst.
common_mistakes: Confusing mainmast, the central mast, with mainsail, the sail attached to it.
Saying main mast as two words in technical writing, where mainmast is the standard form.

senses.definition: To invent or fabricate (a story, claim, etc.).
senses.example: He was a great storyteller and could make up a story on the spot.

senses.definition: To invent, to imagine, to concoct.
senses.example: He was a great storyteller and could make up a story on the spot.

senses.definition: To constitute the components of a whole.
senses.example: Quartz and feldspar make up most of the granite in this quarry.

senses.definition: To compensate, to fill in, to catch up.
senses.example: He can make up the time next week.

senses.definition: To compensate for (a deficiency, defect, etc.); to supply (something missing).
senses.example: He can make up the time next week.

senses.definition: To compensate (for).
senses.example: What I lack in patience, I make up for in drive.

senses.definition: To put together (a substance, material, garment, medicine, etc.) into a specific form; to assemble.
senses.example: I can make up a batch of stew in a few minutes, but it will take a few hours to cook.

senses.definition: To constitute, to compose.
senses.example: Ten members make up the committee, and each serves a three-year term.

senses.definition: To assemble, to prepare.
senses.example: I can make up a batch of stew in a few minutes, but it will take a few hours to cook.

senses.definition: To compile or draw up (a list, document, etc.).
senses.example: She made up a list of the questions for tomorrow's interviews.

senses.definition: To prepare (someone) for a theatrical performance by means of costume, cosmetics, etc.
senses.example: The makeup artist made up the actor as an elderly man for the play.

senses.definition: To apply cosmetics.
senses.example: Let's leave as soon as I make up my face.

senses.definition: To apply cosmetics or makeup to (a face, facial feature).
senses.example: Let's leave as soon as I make up my face.

senses.definition: To make peace, to settle a dispute.
senses.example: They fight a lot, but they always manage to make up.

senses.definition: To resolve or settle an argument, dispute, conflict, or fight (e.g. with someone).
senses.example: They fight a lot, but they always manage to make up.

senses.definition: To arrange, to advance.
senses.example: The runner made up two seconds on the leader in the final lap.

senses.definition: To arrange (a marriage); to organize (a treaty).
senses.example: The matchmaker tried to make up a marriage between the two families' children.

senses.definition: To draw near to, approach to.
senses.example: Dark clouds were making up fast, so we hurried toward the cabin.

senses.definition: To make social or romantic advances to; to pay court to.
senses.example: He spent the whole evening trying to make up to her at the dance.

senses.definition: To build, to complete.
senses.example: The crew made up the new bridge's deck in just three weeks.

core.definition: To become friends again after a quarrel, or to reconcile after an argument.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on up, and the first word make is lighter. Say the k of make clearly and link it into the next word, mayk-UP.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes restoring a friendly relationship, though it can also mean inventing a story, which is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say we made up after a fight, which means they reconciled. Make up can also mean to invent a story or excuse (a negative sense), to form the parts of a whole (Ten players make up the team), or to compensate for missed work. Context usually makes the meaning clear, so listen for the situation.

distinctions.note: Reconcile is more formal and emphasizes restoring a relationship; make up is informal and common in everyday speech.
Invent means to create something new; make up in the invention sense often implies a false story or excuse.

examples.everyday: My sister and I had a huge argument last week, but we made up over dinner last night.
examples.professional: We need to make up the lost time on the migration, so I'd like the team to meet early tomorrow.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of friendship suggests that friends make up after conflict because the bond rests on virtue rather than on convenience.

nuance.analogy: Making up is like repairing a torn sweater: the tear is still there, but the two sides are sewn together again.
nuance.etymology: Make comes from Old English macian; up is from Old English upp, above or toward the top.
common_mistakes: Using make up with a preposition in the reconciliation sense; you make up with someone, not make up someone.
Missing the sense change: make up a story means to invent it, which is not the same as making up after a fight.

make-up.etymology: From Middle English *maken up*, equivalent to *make* + *up*.

conversation.text: He made up an excuse for being late.
That's not true, you're making it up!
They had a fight, but they made up the next day.
Women make up half of our engineering team.
Can I make up the test next week?
He made up an excuse so he wouldn't have to come.
I'm sorry I missed your birthday. Let me make it up to you.

senses.definition: Not formed correctly; misshapen; deformed.

core.definition: Not formed correctly; misshapen, deformed, or badly built from the start.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -FORM-, and the word ends in one syllable with the final d sound, so do not add an extra vowel. Pronounce the r after the vowel clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use malformed mostly for objects, documents, or biological features that are not built or shaped correctly, such as a malformed file or a malformed heart valve. For a person's body, they often prefer deformed or born with a condition, which can sound more sensitive. In a technical sense, a malformed request or query means one that does not follow the required structure.

distinctions.note: Deformed usually describes a visible change in shape that often happens to something that was once normal, while malformed describes something that was never formed correctly.
Misshapen is a plain descriptive word for an unusual or unattractive shape, while malformed suggests a flaw in how the thing was made or developed.

examples.everyday: The pizza box came in malformed, with the corners crushed in.
examples.professional: The API returns an error when the request body is malformed or missing a required field.
examples.analytical: A malformed argument is one whose conclusion does not follow from its premises, even if its individual claims seem reasonable.

nuance.analogy: A malformed object is like a cookie cut from dough that was folded wrong before baking, so it never comes out in the right shape.
nuance.etymology: From mal- (bad) plus formed, past participle of form, from Latin formare.
common_mistakes: Confusing malformed with malfunctioning; malformed refers to shape or structure, while malfunctioning refers to how something works.
Stressing the first syllable, as in MAL-formed, instead of the second syllable.

core.definition: A place in the Sinai wilderness where the Israelites found bitter water, and a Hebrew word meaning bitter, also a name Naomi takes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The r is clearly pronounced in American speech, and the final a is a weak uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in ordinary use, but emotionally charged in the story of Naomi, where it represents bitterness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Marah mainly in Bible study and church teaching. In conversation, people usually mention it when discussing Exodus or the book of Ruth. Use it as a place name or the name Mara.

examples.everyday: We read about Marah in Exodus last night, where the water was too bitter to drink.
examples.professional: In my lesson on Exodus, I explain why Marah matters for the wilderness journey.
examples.analytical: The bitter waters of Marah in Exodus 15 frame the wilderness as a testing ground for trust.

nuance.analogy: Like a sip of water so bitter that you cannot drink it until someone shows you how to change it.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew marah, 'bitter'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as Mar-AH with stress on the second syllable
Confusing Marah the place with Mara the name, which are closely related but used differently
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word marah means bitter. In Exodus 15:23 (RSV), the Israelites cannot drink the water at Marah because it is bitter. In Exodus 15:25 (RSV), Moses cries to the Lord, who shows him a tree that makes the water sweet. In Ruth 1:20 (RSV), Naomi asks to be called Mara because the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her.

senses.definition: To increase the price of something between its wholesale and retail phase.
senses.example: The shop marks up furniture about 100 percent before it reaches the showroom floor.

senses.definition: To add coding to text so that it will display properly on a computer.
senses.example: The editor asked me to mark up the manuscript in XML so the web page displays correctly.

senses.definition: To beat and bruise (someone).
senses.example: The bouncer marked up the drunk man who had insulted his friend near the bar.

core.definition: To raise a product's selling price above what it cost the seller, in order to earn a profit.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'up', so say 'mark UP'. The vowel in 'up' is the short 'uh' sound, and the final p is quiet in quick speech, so it sounds like 'mark-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business; it can sound negative when customers feel prices are unfairly high.
nuance.usage_note: In American retail and business, mark up is the normal verb for setting a price above cost, and markup is the noun for the amount added. Retailers may mark up goods heavily, so customers may feel the price is inflated. In publishing and software, mark up means adding tags or comments to text, as in marking up a document in HTML. Do not use it to mean beat up, which is not current American usage.

distinctions.note: Mark down means lowering a price, while mark up means raising it.
Upcharge is informal for an extra fee on a service, while mark up refers to the price set on a product.
Edit changes the content of a text, while mark up adds comments or codes without changing the wording.

examples.everyday: The gas station marks up its coffee a lot, so I usually bring my own.
examples.professional: We marked up the hardware by forty percent to cover installation and support.
examples.analytical: Her analysis shows how markup reflects market power, not only the cost of production.

nuance.analogy: It is like adding a layer on top of a base cost, as a tip is added to a restaurant bill.
nuance.etymology: From mark (Old English mearc) and up (Old English upp).
common_mistakes: Writing the verb as one word; the verb is mark up, while the noun markup is one word.
Confusing mark up (raise a price) with mark down (lower a price).

senses.definition: Of, or relating to Mark the Evangelist.

core.definition: Relating to Mark the Evangelist or to the Gospel of Mark, the second book of the New Testament.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAR-kuhn, and pronounce the r clearly. The final syllable is reduced to a weak 'uhn', not a full 'an' as in 'can'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly; it has no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Markan almost only in academic, theological and scholarly writing about the Gospel of Mark. In conversation people say the Gospel of Mark or Mark's account. Terms like Markan priority, the view that Mark was written first, are standard in seminars and commentaries.

distinctions.note: Matthean refers to the Gospel of Matthew, not the Gospel of Mark.
Lukan refers to the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles.
Johannine refers to the Gospel of John and the letters traditionally linked with John.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study this week is on the Markan account of Jesus calming the storm.
examples.professional: In the seminar, she argued for Markan priority, the view that Mark was written before Matthew and Luke.
examples.analytical: The Markan redaction of the parable shows the evangelist emphasizing the messianic secret.

nuance.analogy: It is like a first draft of a story that later writers revised and expanded.
nuance.etymology: From Mark, from Latin Marcus, with the adjectival suffix -an.
common_mistakes: Saying MAR-kan with a long a or stressing the second syllable.
Using Markan to mean marked or marking; the adjective refers only to the Gospel or the evangelist.
nuance.biblical_note: Mark is the second Gospel in the New Testament and is traditionally linked with John Mark, a companion of Peter and Paul. The Greek name is Markos, the Greek form of the Latin Marcus. Acts 12:12 identifies a John called Mark in Jerusalem. Acts 15:37-39 describes a dispute between Paul and Barnabas over whether to take John Mark on a mission. 1 Peter 5:13 mentions Mark in connection with Peter.

senses.definition: The condition of a martyr; the death or suffering of a martyr; the death or suffering on account of adherence to the Christian faith, or to any cause.
Extreme suffering, affliction; torment; torture, especially without reason.

core.definition: The suffering or death of a person who is killed or persecuted for holding to their religious faith or a principle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak, reduced sound, and the ending is a soft 'dum' with a schwa, not a full 'dam'.

nuance.connotation: Usually solemn and respectful, though it can be ironic in casual speech about someone exaggerating hardship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use martyrdom mostly in religious, historical and political discussions, such as talking about civil rights leaders. In everyday speech it can be used teasingly about someone who makes a show of suffering. A natural response is to agree lightly or change the subject.

distinctions.note: Sacrifice is giving something up for others, usually not to death; martyrdom specifically involves suffering or death for a faith or principle.
Suffering is any pain; martyrdom implies it is chosen or endured for a cause.

examples.everyday: My grandmother talks about her years of martyrdom at the family reunion, but she always cooks for everyone anyway.
examples.professional: The company's board treated the founder's resignation as a kind of martyrdom, which made it hard to discuss the real problems.
examples.analytical: Christian theology has long debated whether martyrdom must be undertaken freely or whether suffering for faith is enough to make a person a martyr.

nuance.analogy: Martyrdom is like a flame that burns brightest when the wind is strongest, its light becoming a witness to others.
nuance.etymology: From Greek martyrion, meaning witness, through Late Latin martyrium.
common_mistakes: Confusing martyrdom with simple suffering.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'dome' sound.

martyrdom.etymology: From Middle English *martyrdome*, *martirdom*, *marterdom*, from Old English *martyrdōm* (“martyrdom”), corresponding to *martyr* + *dom*.

senses.definition: Enrollment in a college or university.
A pass in some university examinations.
senses.example: She needed a strong pass in matriculation to qualify for the university in Johannesburg.

core.definition: The formal admission or enrollment of a student into a college or university, often marked by an official ceremony or registration.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on LAY, the fourth syllable, with the early syllables reduced to weak vowels. Non-native speakers often stress the first or second syllable, saying MAT-ri-cu-lay-shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to an official step in education and carries no negative associations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'matriculation' mainly in formal academic contexts, such as admissions policies, ceremonies and official letters. In everyday speech they say 'enrollment' or 'starting college'. The second sense, a pass in some university examinations, is used in India and other countries with British-style systems, not commonly in the US.

distinctions.note: Enrollment is the everyday American term for signing up for classes, while matriculation is a more formal term for official admission into a degree program.
Admission means being accepted by a school, while matriculation is the step of actually joining and becoming a registered student.
Graduation is the completion of a program, the opposite end of a student's academic path from matriculation.

examples.everyday: My mom cried at my matriculation, which was basically just the first day of college with a fancy name.
examples.professional: Please confirm your enrollment details, since matriculation records feed directly into our financial aid system.
examples.analytical: Matriculation marks the moment a student formally joins the academic community and takes on its rights and obligations.

nuance.analogy: Matriculation is like signing the guest book at a new club: it is the moment your name officially enters the membership.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin matriculatio, enrollment in a register, from matricula, a register.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying MAT-ri-cu-LAY-shun or ma-TRIK-yoo-lay-shun.
Using matriculation for graduation, which is the opposite event at the end of a program.

senses.definition: In a meaningful or significant manner.

core.definition: In a way that is significant, valuable, or clearly connected to a purpose, rather than in a superficial or symbolic way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MEE. The -ful- part is reduced to 'fuh', and -ly is a light 'lee' at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests effort or substance, and can sound slightly formal in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use meaningfully in workplace language, education, and discussions of community or relationships, as in 'engage meaningfully' or 'contribute meaningfully'. In casual conversation people often say 'really' or 'in a real way' instead. It is rarely used to mean 'with meaning' in a poetic sense.

distinctions.note: Significantly often refers to size or measurable difference, while meaningfully refers to value or depth of engagement.
Substantially means in a large amount or degree, while meaningfully focuses on whether something matters or has real purpose.

examples.everyday: We talked for hours, but we didn't really connect meaningfully until the end.
examples.professional: We need to engage customers meaningfully, not just send them another survey.
examples.analytical: The argument fails because its key terms are not used meaningfully across both premises.

nuance.analogy: Meaningfully is like a handshake that is firm and sincere, rather than a quick wave.
nuance.etymology: From meaningful plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Placing it awkwardly before the verb, as in 'We meaningfully talked'; use 'We talked meaningfully' or 'We had a meaningful talk'.
Using it when you only mean 'a lot'; 'meaningfully' is about value, not quantity.

senses.definition: The view or doctrine that the world can be improved through human effort (often understood as an intermediate outlook between optimism and pessimism).

core.definition: The belief that the world can be improved through human effort, lying between optimism and pessimism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MEEL. The final -ism is a reduced 'um' sound, not 'izm' as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive to neutral; it suggests a hopeful but realistic view of progress.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use meliorism mainly in philosophy, history of ideas and religious studies. In everyday talk they would say a hopeful view or belief in progress. The word is often used in discussions about social reform and the nature of human progress.

distinctions.note: Optimism expects good outcomes without much effort, while meliorism holds that human action can improve the world.
Progressivism is a political movement, while meliorism is a philosophical view about the possibility of improvement.

examples.everyday: My grandfather had a quiet kind of meliorism: he believed things could get better if people worked at them.
examples.professional: The leadership team takes a meliorist view, believing that steady process changes will improve outcomes over time.
examples.analytical: Dewey's meliorism rejects both utopian hope and despair, insisting that social conditions can be improved through intelligent inquiry.

nuance.analogy: Meliorism is like a gardener's outlook: the soil is not perfect, but careful work makes the garden better each season.
nuance.etymology: From Latin melior, 'better', with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing meliorism with optimism; meliorism requires effort, while optimism only expects good things.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable as 'mee-lee-OR-iz-um'.

senses.definition: A proponent of meliorism.
senses.example: My grandfather was a meliorist who believed each generation would leave the world better.

senses.definition: Of or relating to meliorism.
senses.example: Her meliorist outlook shaped how she approached poverty, education, and public health.

senses.definition: Supporting the principles of meliorism.
senses.example: The meliorist reformers argued that careful planning could steadily improve society through reasoned effort.

core.definition: A person who believes the world can be gradually made better through human effort, rather than being either perfect or doomed to decline.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MEE. The middle syllables 'lee-uh-r' blend quickly, so the 'or' sound is reduced to a light 'uh-r' rather than a full 'or'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a hopeful but realistic view of progress, and it can sound slightly naive if the speaker ignores obstacles.
nuance.usage_note: This term appears mainly in philosophy, intellectual history, and academic writing. Americans rarely use it in everyday talk, where they would say someone is 'hopeful' or an 'optimist'. In academic contexts, it is a precise label for someone who believes in incremental improvement.

distinctions.note: An optimist expects good outcomes in general, while a meliorist believes improvement happens only through effort and step by step change.
A pessimist expects things to get worse, whereas a meliorist believes progress is possible but never guaranteed.
A perfectionist wants flawless results, while a meliorist accepts imperfect progress as real progress.

examples.professional: As a meliorist, I believe we can reduce bias in our models through repeated testing and small corrections.
examples.analytical: The meliorist reads history as a record of gradual improvement rather than cyclical decline or inevitable progress.

nuance.analogy: Like a gardener who expects a harvest only after steady weeding and watering, never by wishing alone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin melior, 'better', with the suffix '-ist' for a follower or believer.
common_mistakes: Using 'meliorist' as a synonym for 'optimist', which is looser and less specific.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'meli-OR-ist'.
Confusing it with 'meliorate', the verb, when a noun for the person is needed.

senses.definition: A drama abounding in romantic sentiment and agonizing situations, with a musical accompaniment only in parts which are especially thrilling or pathetic.
senses.example: The old theater staged a melodrama about a banished heiress and her faithful suitor.

senses.definition: A passage in which the orchestra plays a somewhat descriptive accompaniment, while the actor speaks.
senses.example: The grave-digging scene in Beethoven's “Fidelio” has much melodrama.

senses.definition: Any situation or action which is blown out of proportion.
senses.example: Her brother's simple question about dinner turned into a melodrama about his betrayal.

core.definition: A story or situation with exaggerated emotion, sentimental plot, and dramatic, overly intense events.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MEL, and the last syllable is weak. In General American the 'a' in 'drama' is /ɑ/, the same vowel as in 'father'. Say the final syllable as 'muh', not 'mah'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly critical. It suggests exaggeration and overdone emotion, though it can describe an enjoyable entertainment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use melodrama about soap operas, dramatic films, and people who overreact. Calling someone's behavior 'melodrama' can sound dismissive, so use it carefully with friends. 'Drama' is the everyday word for a conflict or emotional scene.

distinctions.note: Drama is a general word for a play, film, or emotional situation; melodrama adds an exaggerated, sentimental quality.
Tragedy is serious and profound in its treatment of suffering, while melodrama is sensational and overwrought.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the argument over the parking spot turned into pure melodrama.
examples.professional: Let's keep the status update factual; this incident doesn't need melodrama in the email.
examples.analytical: The novel slides into melodrama when it depends on coincidence to resolve moral conflict.

nuance.analogy: Like a movie trailer that makes every moment seem like the biggest moment of your life.
nuance.etymology: From Greek melos (song) plus drama (play, action), originally a play with music.
common_mistakes: Using it for any drama; for a simple conflict, 'drama' is more natural.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'mah' instead of a weak 'muh'.

senses.definition: The ability of the brain to record information or impressions with the facility of recalling them later, usually at will.
senses.example: Memory is a facility common to all animals.

senses.definition: A record of a thing or an event stored and available for later use by an organism.
senses.example: I have no memory of that event.

senses.definition: The part of a computer that stores variable executable code or data (RAM) or unalterable executable code or default data (ROM).
senses.example: This data passes from the CPU to the memory.

senses.definition: The time within which past events can be or are remembered.
senses.example: in recent memory

senses.definition: Of a material, which returns to its original shape when heated.
senses.example: memory metal

senses.definition: Synonym of pelmanism (“memory card game”).
senses.example: We played memory on rainy afternoons, flipping cards until every matching pair was found.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) A term of venery for a social group of elephants, normally called a herd.
senses.example: A memory of elephants drifted slowly toward the watering hole at dusk.

core.definition: The mental ability to store past experiences, facts, or skills and bring them back to mind when needed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the last two syllables are weak, so the second vowel is a reduced schwa and the final sound is a short ee. Keep the r clear, since American English is rhotic, and do not stretch it into MEE-mor-ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general use. It turns negative in phrases like 'my memory is failing' or 'bad memory', which imply forgetfulness or decline.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I have a good memory' or 'if my memory serves me right' in everyday talk, and 'from memory' for reciting something without notes. 'In memory of' is standard on gravestones and plaques. In casual speech, people often say 'remember' as a verb instead, so 'I don't remember' is more natural than 'I don't have memory of that'.

distinctions.note: Recall is the act of bringing something back to mind, while memory is the storage and the general ability that makes recall possible.
Remembrance is more formal and emotional, used for honoring someone who has died, while memory is the everyday word for the mental faculty.
In computing, memory usually means fast working storage like RAM, while storage means longer-term disks or drives.

examples.everyday: Sorry, my memory is terrible, so what was your name again?
examples.professional: The server's memory usage jumped after the last deployment, so we need to check for a leak.
examples.analytical: Husserl distinguished retention from recollection, which suggests that memory is not one faculty but a structured temporal process.

nuance.analogy: Memory is like a filing cabinet, though most of us have a few drawers jammed shut.
nuance.etymology: From Latin memoria, from memor, meaning mindful or remembering.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I have memory of that day' instead of 'I have a memory of that day' or 'I remember that day'.
Pronouncing the first syllable as long MEE or the middle syllable as full vowels, rather than MEM-uh-ree.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew verb zākar means to remember, and the Greek anamnēsis means remembrance, though Scripture rarely uses an abstract word for memory. Exodus 20:8 asks Israel to keep the sabbath in mind, Deuteronomy 8:2 tells Israel to recall how God led them through the wilderness, and Luke 22:19 has Jesus telling his disciples to do this in remembrance of him.

memory.etymology: From Anglo-Norman *memorie*, Old French *memoire* etc. from Latin *memoria* (“the faculty of remembering, remembrance, memory, a historical account”), from *memor* (“mindful, remembering”), from Proto-Indo-European **mer-*, related to *μέρμερος*…

senses.definition: In a mental manner; an idea thought out in one's mind, as opposed to an idea spoken orally.
senses.example: mentally capable

core.definition: In terms of the mind or mental state; in one's head, or with respect to thinking, concentration or mental health.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a weak schwa, so the t is quick and often nearly silent. Avoid stressing the second syllable (men-TAL-ly) or pronouncing it as a full 'tal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a mental state or process, and it can be positive (mentally strong) or negative (mentally exhausted) depending on the adjective it modifies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mentally' most often before adjectives such as 'mentally tough,' 'mentally exhausted,' or 'mentally prepared.' For a condition, 'mental health' or 'a person with a mental health condition' is more respectful and current than 'mentally ill,' which many people now find dated. In casual talk, you might say 'I'm mentally done for today' to mean you are too tired to think any more.

distinctions.note: 'Mentally' usually refers to thinking, focus or cognitive state, while 'psychologically' refers more broadly to emotions, personality and behavior.
'Emotionally' concerns feelings, while 'mentally' concerns thinking and mental capacity; a person can be emotionally drained but mentally sharp.

examples.everyday: After that twelve-hour shift, I'm mentally exhausted, so let's just order pizza and watch something easy.
examples.professional: The team is mentally prepared for the launch, but we still need the documentation finished before Thursday.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that we can mentally represent a concept in its universal form before we ever encounter a particular instance of it.

nuance.analogy: Mentally is like a phone's working memory: it holds only so many open tasks at once, and when too many are running, everything slows down.
nuance.etymology: From mental, from Latin mentalis, from mens (mentis), mind; -ly forms an adverb.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in 'men-TAL-ly'.
Confusing 'mentally' with 'mentioned' or 'mental' as a noun; 'mental' is an adjective, so 'mentally' describes how something is thought or felt.

senses.definition: Without any other reason etc. only, just, and nothing more.

core.definition: Only, just, and nothing more; used to say something is no more important or serious than it seems.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the vowel is short, like 'mirror'. Don't stretch the first vowel to 'MEER-lee', and make the last syllable a light 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly diminishing; often used to downplay something or to correct a misunderstanding.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'merely' in conversation and writing to say that something is simply that and no more. It is more formal than 'just' and 'only', but it is common in both speech and writing. Often a reply is 'Oh, okay' or 'I understand'. It works well with 'not merely... but also' for contrast.

distinctions.note: Only is more general and can limit by number or time; merely stresses that something is small or unimpressive.
Just is more conversational and common in speech; merely sounds more formal and deliberate.
Simply can mean 'plainly' or 'easily'; merely focuses on the limited importance of something.

examples.everyday: I'm not mad, I'm merely disappointed you didn't call.
examples.professional: The dashboard does not merely report numbers; it flags the anomalies that need action.
examples.analytical: Faith, on this account, is not merely assent to propositions but a trusting relation to a person.

nuance.analogy: Merely is like a light dusting of snow: it is there, but it does not change the whole landscape.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'mere' (adjective) with the adverbial suffix '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'merely' where 'only' with a number is more natural, such as 'only three people came', not 'merely three people came'.
Stressing the second syllable, or pronouncing the first vowel as 'ay'.
Placing 'merely' awkwardly; it usually goes before the word it limits.

senses.definition: In full celestial meridian: a great circle passing through the poles of the celestial sphere and the zenith for a particular point on the Earth's surface.

In full terrestrial meridian: a great circle on the Earth's surface, passing through the geographic poles (the terrestrial North Pole and South Pole); also, half of such a circle extending from pole to pole, all points of which have the same longitude.
The place on the celestial meridian where it is crossed by the sun or a star at its highest point.
The highest or most developed point, or most splendid stage, of something; culmination, peak, zenith.
Chiefly followed by of: the middle period of someone's life, when they are at their full abilities or strength; one's prime.
A ring or half-ring with markings in which an artificial globe is installed and may spin.
A line passing through the poles of any sphere; a notional line on the surface of a curved or round body (in particular, an eyeball).
The south. Midday, noon.
The south.
Midday, noon.
A midday rest; a siesta.
A particular area or situation considered as having a specific characteristic or identity; also, the characteristics, habits, or tastes of a specific group, locale, etc.

Any of the pathways on the body along which chi or qi (life force) is thought to flow and, therefore, the acupoints are distributed; especially, one of twelve such pathways associated with organs of the body.
The size of type between double great primer and canon, standardized as 44-point.
To cause an object to reach the meridian or highest point of (something).
Of a celestial body: to reach its meridian.
Relating to a meridian (in various senses); meridional.
Relating to the culmination or highest point.
Relating to the south; meridional, southern.

core.definition: An imaginary north-south line on Earth through both poles, or the highest point a celestial body reaches in the sky.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, RID. Reduce the first syllable to a quick 'muh', and say the last two syllables lightly, with 'ee-un' rather than 'ee-ahn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in geography, navigation and astronomy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'meridian' mainly in geography, astronomy, navigation and science education, as in the 'prime meridian' at Greenwich. In everyday talk, people say 'longitude line' or 'the line of longitude.' The word also has a figurative sense, meaning a peak or high point, that appears in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Longitude is the angular measure of east-west position; a meridian is the actual north-south line of constant longitude.
A parallel is a line of latitude running east-west; a meridian runs north-south through the poles.

examples.everyday: The prime meridian runs through Greenwich, so the map shows that line in a straight north-south direction.
examples.professional: Our GPS software uses the prime meridian as the reference for longitude in every coordinate calculation.
examples.analytical: In classical astronomy, a star reaches its greatest altitude when it crosses the local meridian, which defines midday for an observer.

nuance.analogy: Like a line of longitude drawn on a globe that connects the North and South Poles, a meridian is a fixed guide for direction on the Earth.
nuance.etymology: From Latin meridianus, 'of midday', from meridies, 'midday', from medius and dies.
common_mistakes: Saying 'MER-id-ee-an' with the stress on the first syllable.
Confusing meridian with 'median', which means middle or average.

senses.definition: Clipping of metagame.
senses.example: I don't think the character will be part of the meta even with the recent buffs.

senses.definition: An informal but widely adopted practice in a given field; a de facto standard.
senses.example: Each video sharing platform's community has a meta on how long videos should be.

senses.definition: Clipping of metaoidioplasty.
senses.example: Her surgeon explained the recovery timeline for meta, which she had scheduled for March.

senses.definition: Clipping of metamour.
senses.example: She told her meta that they both loved hiking on weekends.

senses.definition: Clipping of metanalysis: metanalysis or metacommentary focused on media, fandom, or related topics, typically presented as an essay or dialogue.
senses.example: The podcast's meta examined fan debates about the show's ending in a long essay.

senses.definition: Boundary marker.
senses.example: The old stone meta marked the boundary between the two villages.

senses.definition: (historical) Either of the conical columns at each end of an Ancient Roman circus.
senses.example: Chariots raced around the spina, rounding the bronze meta at each end of the Circus Maximus.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Self-referential; structured analogously (structured by relationships), but at a higher level.
senses.example: Suppose you have a genie that grants you three wishes. If you wish for infinite wishes, that is a meta wish.

senses.definition: Prominent in the metagame; effective and frequently used in competitive gameplay.
senses.example: I don't think the character will be meta even with the recent buffs.

core.definition: The strategy or build that players have converged on as the most effective in a game; the de facto standard that everyone uses.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is short, like the e in "met." The final a is a reduced schwa, so avoid pronouncing it as "ee."

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Gamers and tech workers use meta informally to describe what works best right now, usually in competitive play. Capitalized Meta usually refers to Meta Platforms, the company, so context matters. In academic and technical writing, meta also appears as a prefix meaning "about itself," but that is a different sense.

distinctions.note: Standard is a more formal and official word for accepted practice, while meta is informal and specific to what works best in a game or field right now.
A trend is a general direction over time, while the meta is a set of strategies that players actively converge on as most effective.

examples.everyday: Is that build still the meta, or did the last patch nerf it?
examples.professional: Our team has settled on the meta for dashboard design, so we all use the same templates.
examples.analytical: The top-ranked players converge on the meta, and any new strategy must beat it to become standard.

nuance.analogy: Like a fashion season in which everyone dresses the same way until the next trend arrives.
nuance.etymology: Clipped from metagame, from Greek meta, "with, after, beyond," with game.
common_mistakes: Using a long e in the first syllable, as in MEE-tuh
Confusing the gaming sense with the prefix sense meaning "about itself"

senses.definition: A nutritional supplement.
senses.example: The gym trainer recommended a metabolic to help with my energy during morning workouts.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to metabolism.
senses.example: metabolic activity

core.definition: Relating to metabolism, the chemical processes by which the body or a living cell converts food into energy and building materials.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, -BAH-, which uses the American 'ah' vowel shared by cot and caught. Reduce the first two syllables, and don't stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical in science; in everyday American talk it can sound like diet and fitness claims, which may be positive or hype.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use metabolic in medicine, nutrition and fitness, as in metabolic rate, metabolic syndrome or metabolic health. In casual talk people often say 'my metabolism is slow,' not 'my metabolic rate is low.' The noun form, meaning a supplement, is a marketing usage and is less common in serious discussions.

distinctions.note: Metabolism is the noun for the process itself; metabolic is the adjective describing things related to that process.
Metabolic syndrome is a specific group of risk conditions, while metabolic alone is a general adjective.

examples.everyday: My doctor said my metabolic numbers are fine, so I don't need to change my diet much.
examples.professional: The nutrition team measured the metabolic response to the new diet across all participants in the study.
examples.analytical: A metabolic model of cellular energy must account for both the supply of substrates and the regulation of enzyme activity.

nuance.analogy: A metabolic process is like a kitchen: raw ingredients come in, are processed, and turn into fuel and materials, all while the cook keeps the stove running.
nuance.etymology: From Greek metabolē, 'change,' via metabolikos, 'changeable.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'MET-uh-bol-ik' instead of the third.
Using metabolic as a noun for metabolism in ordinary sentences.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as a clear 'ah' instead of a reduced schwa.

senses.definition: A grinding apparatus for substances such as grains, seeds, etc. (Some are small and simple, and some are large and complex.)
senses.example: Pepper has a stronger flavor when it is ground straight from a mill.

senses.definition: The building housing such a grinding apparatus; also, any similar building that houses a similarly material activity (such as weaving, fulling, dying, etc.); the place of business comprising such a building and its outbuildings and grounds.
senses.example: My great-grandfather worked in a mill. He filled the flour sacks and then carried and loaded them.

senses.definition: A machine used for expelling the juice, sap, etc. from vegetable tissues by pressure, or by pressure in combination with a grinding, or cutting process; any similar apparatus that otherwise processes.
senses.example: a cider mill; a cane mill

senses.definition: A machine for grinding and polishing.
senses.example: a lapidary mill

senses.definition: A milling machine for machining of solid metal, wood, or plastic.
senses.example: Several machinists were busy operating the lathes, mills, and drill presses on the shop floor.

senses.definition: A milling cutter used on such a machine.
senses.example: After the drilling and tapping operations, we come in with a mill and do some contouring.

senses.definition: A manufacturing plant for paper, steel, textiles, flooring, and some other kinds of materials.
senses.example: Once the billet gets through the 56-inch mill, it is ready for reheating.

senses.definition: The building complex housing such a plant; the place of business comprising such buildings and their grounds.
senses.example: My grandfather worked in a mill. He operated machinery, did maintenance, and drove forklifts.

senses.definition: An establishment that handles a certain type of situation or procedure routinely, or produces large quantities of an item without much regard to quality. (The notion of churning out massive amounts indiscriminately underlies the figurative metaphor.)
senses.example: Those shysters selling the purebreds are running quite a mill over there, eh?

senses.definition: An institution or pseudo-institutional business awarding credentials (such as diplomas, degrees, certificates, or certifications) of either dubious value or fraudulent nature; one selling essays or other documents for the buyers (usually students) to fraudulently pass off as their own.
senses.example: Those shysters cranking out the "IT training certificates" are running quite a mill over there, eh?

senses.definition: An engine.
senses.example: Under the hood is a mill that you and I can't afford — a nitrous-blown hemi with custom heads.

senses.definition: A hardened steel roller with a design in relief, used for imprinting a reversed copy of the design in a softer metal, such as copper.
senses.example: The engraver pressed the steel mill into copper to transfer the design.

senses.definition: An excavation in rock, transverse to the workings, from which material for filling is obtained.
senses.example: They pulled me off the main crew and had me digging in the mill.

senses.definition: A passage underground through which ore is shot.
senses.example: The geologists were responsible for keeping the work within the mill.

senses.definition: The raised or ridged edge or surface made in milling anything, such as a coin or screw.
senses.example: Run your thumb along the mill of the coin to feel its raised edge.

senses.definition: A typewriter used to transcribe messages received.
senses.example: The clerk used a mill to transcribe every telegram that arrived overnight.

senses.definition: One thousandth part.
senses.example: The U.S. has never minted a mill coin, but the Coinage Act of 1792 describes this and other subdivisions of the U.S. dollar.

senses.definition: One thousandth of a US dollar, one-hundredth of a dime or one-tenth of a cent.
senses.example: The U.S. has never minted a mill coin, but the Coinage Act of 1792 describes this and other subdivisions of the U.S. dollar.

senses.definition: One thousandth part in millage rates of property tax.
senses.example: They predict that the rate will probably go up by several mills next year.

senses.definition: Clipping of millimeter.
senses.example: For this task, I prefer the plastic bars that are 10 mills in diameter.

senses.definition: Clipping of milliliter.
A line of three matching pieces in nine men's morris and related games.
senses.example: In nine men's morris, forming a mill of three pieces lets you remove an opponent's piece.

senses.definition: Discarding a card from one's deck.
senses.example: The opponent chose to mill two cards from her library.

senses.definition: A strategy centered on depleting the opponent's deck.
senses.example: Her deck relied on a mill strategy to empty the opponent's library.

senses.definition: A military prison, either guardhouse or post prison.
senses.example: He spent some time in the mill after that escapade.

senses.definition: A delousing station: a cootie mill.
senses.example: The soldiers queued at the mill to have their uniforms deloused.

senses.definition: (historical) A prison treadmill.
senses.example: They kept us in line by threatening to put us on the mill twice as long if we complained.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To grind or otherwise process in a mill or other machine.
senses.example: to mill flour

senses.definition: To shape, polish, dress or finish using a machine.
senses.example: The machinist will mill the aluminum block to fit the new bracket.

senses.definition: To engrave one or more grooves or a pattern around the edge of (a cylindrical object such as a coin).
senses.example: The mint still mills the edges of its coins to deter counterfeiting.

senses.definition: To move about in an aimless fashion.
senses.example: I didn't have much to do, so I just milled around the town looking at the shops.

senses.definition: To cause to mill, or circle around.
senses.example: to mill cattle

senses.definition: To beat; to pound.
senses.example: Heavy rain milled on the tin roof all night long.

senses.definition: To pass through a fulling mill; to full, as cloth.
senses.example: The weaver sent the wool to the village to mill into thick cloth.

senses.definition: To roll (steel, etc.) into bars.
senses.example: The plant can mill the raw steel into bars for construction projects.

senses.definition: To make (drinking chocolate) frothy, as by churning.
senses.example: Grandma would mill the cocoa with hot milk until it foamed.

senses.definition: To undergo hulling.
senses.example: This maize mills well.

senses.definition: To take part in a fistfight; to box.
senses.example: The two boys agreed to mill it out behind the gym after school.

senses.definition: To fill (a winze or interior incline) with broken ore, to be drawn out at the bottom.
senses.example: The crew milled the winze with broken ore before the next blast.

senses.definition: To move (a card) from a deck to the discard pile.
To destroy (a card) due to having a full hand.
To swim underwater.
To swim suddenly in a new direction, or to circle around.

core.definition: A machine or building that grinds grain, wood, metal, or other materials into powder or a finished form.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short i, as in 'mitt', and a light L. Do not stretch it into 'meal' or 'mile'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a physical place or machine, with a traditional, working-class image.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mill for grain mills, sawmills, paper mills, and steel mills. For a small kitchen appliance that grinds coffee or pepper, say grinder. The idiom run-of-the-mill means ordinary and unremarkable, and to go through the mill means to endure hardship.

distinctions.note: A factory assembles or manufactures goods; a mill processes raw material such as grain, wood, or metal.
A grinder is usually a small household appliance; a mill is a larger machine or building used in industry or agriculture.

examples.everyday: We drove past the old grist mill on the way to the lake.
examples.professional: The paper mill runs two shifts to meet the new order.
examples.analytical: Early industrial villages organized their economic lives around the mill, which shaped labor, housing, and family routines.

nuance.analogy: A mill is like a giant blender for raw materials, turning bulk material into a finer, usable form.
